title: Session 5 — Choosing, Comparing and Reporting
text:
Where we are

Sessions 1-4: ordered and nominal outcomes, the assumption, the models
Today: choose between them, show the results, report
By the end you can:

justify ordinal vs multinomial
plot predicted probabilities
judge a model without relying on accuracy
write the methods and results

title: Session 5 — Choosing, Comparing and Reporting
text:
A decision








Question
Answer
Model




Is there a meaningful order?
No
Multinomial logistic



Yes
Ordinal logistic (proportional odds)


Does proportional odds hold (Brant, cut-point ORs)?
Yes
one OR per predictor

title: Session 5 — Choosing, Comparing and Reporting
text:
The same data, two models

a_ord <- MASS::polr(anaemia ~ wealth + tribal, data = mat, Hess = TRUE)
a_mn <- nnet::multinom(factor(anaemia, ordered = FALSE) ~ wealth + tribal, data = mat, trace = FALSE)
c(ordinal = AIC(a_ord), multinomial = AIC(a_mn)) |> round(0)

    ordinal multinomial 
       3200        3170 



The multinomial model has the lower AIC because it frees the tribal effect at each cut-point; it also needs many more parameters (9 vs 5). When proportional odds holds, the ordinal model is simpler and more powerful. When it fails and cannot be relaxed, multinomial is the safe fallback.

title: Session 5 — Choosing, Comparing and Reporting
text:
Probabilities against a predictor

m_ord <- MASS::polr(anaemia ~ wealth + education + bmi + anc_visits + parity + age + tribal + residence, data = mat, Hess = TRUE)
nd <- data.frame(wealth = 1:5, education = factor("Primary", levels = levels(mat$education)), bmi = 20.5, anc_visits = 3, parity = 2, age = 27, tribal = factor("No", levels = c("No", "Yes")), residence = factor("Rural", levels = c("Urban", "Rural")))
cbind(wealth = 1:5, as.data.frame(predict(m_ord, newdata = nd, type = "probs"))) |> pivot_longer(-wealth, names_to = "anaemia", values_to = "probability") |>
  mutate(anaemia = factor(anaemia, levels = levels(mat$anaemia))) |>
  ggplot(aes(wealth, probability, colour = anaemia)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + labs(x = "Wealth quintile", y = "Predicted probability", colour = NULL)


The same idea for the nominal outcome: predicted probabilities of each delivery place across wealth show home falling and private rising.

title: Session 5 — Choosing, Comparing and Reporting
text: Probabilities against a predictor

title: Session 5 — Choosing, Comparing and Reporting
text:
Accuracy is a weak summary

mat$delivery <- relevel(mat$delivery, ref = "Home")
mn <- nnet::multinom(delivery ~ wealth + education + anc_visits + residence + tribal, data = mat, trace = FALSE)
c(model = mean(predict(mn) == mat$delivery), always_most_common = max(prop.table(table(mat$delivery)))) |> round(2)

             model always_most_common 
              0.48               0.32 



The model is right about 48% of the time vs 32% for always guessing the most common place. Covariates shift probabilities but cannot predict an individual’s choice; accuracy ignores the probabilities. Use predicted probabilities, AIC or log-likelihood, and, if prediction is the aim, calibration and proper scoring rules.

title: Session 5 — Choosing, Comparing and Reporting
text:
Wording

Ordinal: “In a proportional-odds model adjusted for education, BMI, antenatal visits, parity, age, tribal group and residence, each higher wealth quintile was associated with 24% lower odds of being in a worse anaemia category (OR 0.76, 95% CI …). The assumption held for all predictors except tribal group, so its effect is reported separately at each cut-point.”


Multinomial: “Compared with home delivery, each wealth quintile increased the relative risk of delivering in a private hospital 2.8-fold (RRR 2.76, 95% CI …).”

title: Session 5 — Choosing, Comparing and Reporting
text:
Reporting checklist

Outcome categories, order, counts; reference category (nominal)
Model and why (ordered or not); software (MASS, nnet, ordinal)
Odds ratios (ordinal) or relative risk ratios (multinomial) with 95% CI; adjustment set
Assumption check (Brant, cut-specific ORs) and what you did
Predicted probabilities for key profiles
Limitations: sparse categories, many parameters, association not cause, self-reported outcomes

title: Session 5 — Choosing, Comparing and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (1/5)

When is the multinomial model a good choice for an ordered outcome?

The sample of women is very small for a model with many parameters
All the predictors in the model are binary variables only
Proportional odds fails for many predictors and cannot be relaxed
The outcome has three ordered categories in the data set

title: Session 5 — Choosing, Comparing and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (2/5)

The multinomial model classifies 48% of women correctly and always guessing the most common place gives 32%. What is the best conclusion?

The model is excellent, since it beats guessing the most common place
Covariates shift probabilities, but accuracy is a weak summary
The model has failed and should be rejected for this use
The two numbers cannot be compared with each other in any way

title: Session 5 — Choosing, Comparing and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (3/5)

Why plot predicted probabilities against a predictor such as wealth?

They give the p-value of the Brant test for the predictor shown
They replace the need for odds ratios in any paper that is written
They show how each category’s probability changes with it
They prove that the effect of the predictor is a causal one

title: Session 5 — Choosing, Comparing and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (4/5)

Which sentence is the best way to report an ordinal result when the assumption holds?

Each higher quintile lowers the anaemia grade by 0.76 of one whole category
Wealthy women have 76% of the anaemia that is found in poor women
Wealth had a significant effect on anaemia because the p-value was small
Each higher quintile went with 24% lower odds of a worse category (OR 0.76)

title: Session 5 — Choosing, Comparing and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (5/5)

What belongs in the limitations of a categorical-outcome analysis?

Sparse categories, many parameters, and association not being cause
The fact that the outcome has more than two categories to model
That odds ratios cannot be reported when there are many categories
That the software used for the analysis was written in the R language

title: Session 5 — Choosing, Comparing and Reporting
text:
Score and take-home
Your score: 

Ordered and the assumption holds: ordinal; fails for one or two: partial; many or no order: multinomial
Show predicted probabilities and plots, not only odds ratios
Do not judge by classification accuracy
Report categories, reference, model, ORs/RRRs with CI, assumption check, limitations

title: Session 3 — Checking Proportional Odds
text:
Where we are

Session 2: one odds ratio per predictor
Today: is that single OR legitimate?
By the end you can:

run and read the Brant test
see a violation with separate binary models
fit a partial proportional-odds model
decide what to do

title: Session 3 — Checking Proportional Odds
text:
The Brant test

m2 <- MASS::polr(anaemia ~ wealth + education + bmi + anc_visits + parity + age + tribal + residence, data = mat, Hess = TRUE)
br <- brant(m2); round(br[, "probability"], 3)

---------------------------------------------------- 
Test for        X2  df  probability 
---------------------------------------------------- 
Omnibus         58.74   20  0
wealth          1.11    2   0.57
educationPrimary    1.44    2   0.49
educationSecondary  1.68    2   0.43
educationHigher 2.74    2   0.25
bmi         0.64    2   0.72
anc_visits      1.33    2   0.52
parity          2.55    2   0.28
age         0.86    2   0.65
tribalYes       39.03   2   0
residenceRural      1.85    2   0.4
---------------------------------------------------- 

H0: Parallel Regression Assumption holds


           Omnibus             wealth   educationPrimary educationSecondary 
             0.000              0.574              0.486              0.433 
   educationHigher                bmi         anc_visits             parity 
             0.254              0.725              0.515              0.279 
               age          tribalYes     residenceRural 
             0.650              0.000              0.396

title: Session 3 — Checking Proportional Odds
text:
Reading the Brant test

Omnibus test: do any predictors violate the assumption?
A p-value per predictor: here tribal group (p about 0); wealth (0.57), education, BMI and the others look fine
With many predictors, expect the occasional small p by chance; look at the effect, not only at p
It warns about sparse cells from continuous predictors: ignore the warning if the results are stable

title: Session 3 — Checking Proportional Odds
text:
See it

cuts <- c("Mild", "Moderate", "Severe")
or_for <- function(v) sapply(cuts, \(k) exp(coef(glm(I(as.numeric(mat$anaemia) >= which(levels(mat$anaemia) == k)) ~ wealth + tribal, family = binomial, data = mat))[v]))
rbind(tribal = or_for("tribalYes"), wealth = or_for("wealth")) |> round(2)

       Mild.tribalYes Moderate.tribalYes Severe.tribalYes
tribal           1.13               1.05             3.23
wealth           0.58               0.60             0.61



Each column is a separate binary logistic model: “mild or worse”, “moderate or worse”, “severe”. Wealth’s OR is the same in all three (about 0.6): proportional odds holds. Tribal’s OR jumps to about 3 for severe anaemia only: it does not.

title: Session 3 — Checking Proportional Odds
text:
Partial proportional odds
Free only the offending predictor (ordinal::clm with nominal =):

m_po  <- ordinal::clm(anaemia ~ wealth + education + bmi + anc_visits + parity + age + tribal + residence, data = mat)
m_ppo <- ordinal::clm(anaemia ~ wealth + education + bmi + anc_visits + parity + age + residence, nominal = ~ tribal, data = mat)
anova(m_po, m_ppo)

Likelihood ratio tests of cumulative link models:
 
      formula:                                                                           
m_po  anaemia ~ wealth + education + bmi + anc_visits + parity + age + tribal + residence
m_ppo anaemia ~ wealth + education + bmi + anc_visits + parity + age + residence         
      nominal: link: threshold:
m_po  ~1       logit flexible  
m_ppo ~tribal  logit flexible  

      no.par    AIC  logLik LR.stat df Pr(>Chisq)    
m_po      13 3134.6 -1554.3                          
m_ppo     15 3101.0 -1535.5  37.575  2  6.927e-09 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

title: Session 3 — Checking Proportional Odds
text:
Reading the comparison

The likelihood-ratio test is very small: freeing tribal improves the fit a lot
All other predictors keep one odds ratio each
Tribal gets a separate effect at each threshold (for a worse category the OR is 1 / exp(coefficient): about 1.0, 0.9 and 2.8)

title: Session 3 — Checking Proportional Odds
text:
Options when the assumption fails







Option
Use when




Partial proportional odds
one or a few predictors violate it


Report cut-point-specific ORs (separate binary models)
simple, transparent


Multinomial model
many violations, or the order is doubtful


Keep the single OR
mild violation, only a summary needed (say so)


Merge categories
a sparse category drives it

title: Session 3 — Checking Proportional Odds
section: Do not report one OR blindly
text:
Do not report one OR blindly

c(single_OR_tribal = round(exp(coef(m_po))[["tribalYes"]], 2))

single_OR_tribal 
            1.11 



The single OR of about 1.1 averages “almost no effect on mild and moderate anaemia” with “a large effect on severe anaemia”. Reporting it hides the finding that matters clinically.

title: Session 3 — Checking Proportional Odds
text:
Self-check quiz (1/5)

The Brant test gives p < 0.001 for tribal group and p = 0.57 for wealth. What does this mean?

Tribal group has no effect while wealth has a very strong effect
Both predictors violate proportional odds, in different patterns
Proportional odds fails for tribal group, not for wealth
The model must be discarded for every one of the predictors in it

title: Session 3 — Checking Proportional Odds
text:
Self-check quiz (2/5)

Separate binary models give tribal ORs of 1.1 (mild or worse), 1.0 (moderate or worse) and 3.2 (severe). What does this show?

The tribal effect is the same at each cut-point, so the model is right
The effect varies across cut-points, so the assumption fails
Severe anaemia was measured incorrectly in the tribal women studied
The sample of tribal women is too large for the test to be valid

title: Session 3 — Checking Proportional Odds
text:
Self-check quiz (3/5)

What does a partial proportional-odds model do?

It drops the problem predictor from the model that is being fitted
It converts the outcome into a binary variable for every woman
It frees the problem predictor, keeping one OR for the rest
It estimates a separate model for each woman in the data

title: Session 3 — Checking Proportional Odds
text:
Self-check quiz (4/5)

A likelihood-ratio test comparing the proportional and the partial model has p < 0.001. What do you conclude?

The proportional-odds model fits better than the partial model does
The two models are identical, so either one may be reported
The predictor must be removed from both of the models being compared
Freeing it improves the fit a lot: the assumption fails

title: Session 3 — Checking Proportional Odds
text:
Self-check quiz (5/5)

Which is the best way to report a predictor that violates proportional odds?

Give its OR at each cut-point and explain the pattern seen
Report the single OR and stay silent about the violation found
Report only the p-value from the Brant test, with no estimate
Delete the predictor from the data so that the model fits again

title: Session 3 — Checking Proportional Odds
text:
Score and take-home
Your score: 

Brant test per predictor + omnibus; see it with binary models at each cut
Partial proportional odds with clm(nominal = ~ x)
Alternatives: cut-specific ORs, multinomial, merge categories
Never report a single OR that hides a violation

title: Session 1 — Categorical Outcomes: Nominal or Ordered?
text:
Where we are

Regression workshop: continuous (linear) and binary (logistic) outcomes
Today: outcomes with three or more categories: anaemia severity, place of delivery, BP stage, disease stage

title: Session 1 — Categorical Outcomes: Nominal or Ordered?
section: Our data: a maternal health survey
text:
Our data: a maternal health survey



1,500 women with a birth in the last 3 years (synthetic, built like an NFHS-type survey)
Anaemia in four ordered levels: None < Mild < Moderate < Severe
Place of delivery in four unordered levels: Home, PHC, Public hospital, Private hospital
Predictors: wealth quintile, education, residence, tribal group, antenatal visits, BMI, parity, age

text:
Nominal or ordered?








Outcome
Type
Model family




Hypertension yes/no
binary
logistic


Anaemia: none, mild, moderate, severe
ordered

Ask: does the order of the categories mean something? Mild anaemia is between none and moderate, so anaemia is ordered. “PHC” is not between “Home” and “Public hospital” in any statistical sense, so delivery place is nominal.

title: Session 1 — Categorical Outcomes: Nominal or Ordered?
text:
Cumulative proportions

round(100 * prop.table(table(mat$anaemia)), 1)


    None     Mild Moderate   Severe 
    54.4     26.5     12.2      6.9 

round(100 * cumsum(prop.table(table(mat$anaemia))), 1)

    None     Mild Moderate   Severe 
    54.4     80.9     93.1    100.0 



The second line is P(Y ≤ k): 81% of women have mild anaemia or better
The proportional-odds model (Session 2) models the log odds of these cumulative probabilities
Nominal outcomes have no cumulative scale: each category is compared with a reference

text:
Anaemia by wealth

round(100 * prop.table(table(mat$wealth, mat$anaemia), 1), 1)

  2 41.3 36.9     14.2    7.7

  4 69.1 20.8      7.3    2.8

ggplot(mat, aes(factor(wealth), fill = anaemia)) + geom_bar(position = "fill") + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "OrRd", direction = -1) +
  labs(x = "Wealth quintile (1 = poorest)", y = "Proportion", fill = NULL)



The share with no anaemia rises from about 30% to 78%, and severe anaemia almost vanishes in the richest quintile. A 100% stacked bar is the standard picture for an ordered outcome.

title: Session 1 — Categorical Outcomes: Nominal or Ordered?
text:
Treating categories as numbers

coef(lm(as.numeric(anaemia) ~ wealth, data = mat))["wealth"]

    wealth 
-0.2395462 




Equal spacing assumed: None to Mild is treated like Moderate to Severe
“-0.24 categories per quintile” is not interpretable and can be misleading at the extremes

title: Session 1 — Categorical Outcomes: Nominal or Ordered?
text:
Dichotomising

Collapsing to “any anaemia vs none” throws away the difference between mild and severe, loses power, and depends on where you cut. Use it for a simple summary, not as the analysis when the ordering is available.

title: Session 1 — Categorical Outcomes: Nominal or Ordered?
text:
Checklist before modelling


Nominal or ordered? (order meaningful?)
Counts per category: the smallest has about 103 women here; very small categories (a few per cent or fewer than about 10 per predictor) make estimates unstable: merge neighbouring categories if it makes clinical sense
Reference category (nominal): choose one that is large and meaningful (Home)
Plan the assumption check (proportional odds)

text:
Self-check quiz (1/5)

Which outcome is ordered, and so suited to an ordinal model?

Place of delivery: home, PHC, or a hospital
Blood group: A, B, AB or O in the patient
Anaemia graded none, mild, moderate or severe
Religion recorded in the survey of households

title: Session 1 — Categorical Outcomes: Nominal or Ordered?
text:
Self-check quiz (2/5)

The cumulative percentages for anaemia are 54, 81, 93 and 100. What does 81 mean?

81% of women have mild anaemia
81% of women have no or mild anaemia
81% of women have at least mild anaemia
The odds of mild anaemia are 81

title: Session 1 — Categorical Outcomes: Nominal or Ordered?
text:
Self-check quiz (3/5)

A linear regression of anaemia coded 1 to 4 on wealth is a poor choice because it…

It cannot produce a coefficient for wealth from the data supplied
It needs a much smaller number of women than the other models do
It assumes equal gaps between the categories in severity
It always gives a larger p-value for wealth than ordinal models do

title: Session 1 — Categorical Outcomes: Nominal or Ordered?
text:
Self-check quiz (4/5)

What is the main cost of dichotomising an ordered outcome into ‘any anaemia’ vs ‘none’?

It makes the outcome nominal and so impossible to model at all
It requires the outcome data to be normally distributed in each group
It changes the direction of the effect in the very large majority of data sets
It discards the mild-severe difference and loses power

title: Session 1 — Categorical Outcomes: Nominal or Ordered?
text:
Self-check quiz (5/5)

What should you check about the categories of an outcome before fitting a model?

That no category is so small that estimates become unstable
That the categories are listed in alphabetical order by name
That every category has exactly the same number of women in it
That the outcome is stored in the data file as a number

title: Session 1 — Categorical Outcomes: Nominal or Ordered?

Your score: 

Ordered or nominal? decides the model family
Ordered: cumulative proportions, 100% stacked bars

title: Session 5 — Reporting and Extensions
text:
The sentence for the paper

“In a negative binomial model with a ward-population offset, adjusted for ward type, previous-month rainfall, time trend and seasonality, the dengue rate in fogged ward-months was 0.66 times that in unfogged ward-months (95% CI 0.54-0.8), a 34% lower rate.”

title: Session 5 — Reporting and Extensions
section: Words that are right and wrong
text:
Words that are right and wrong



Say
Do not say




“rate was 34% lower”
“risk was 34% lower”


“associated with” (observational)
“fogging caused”


“adjusted for …” and list them
“controlling for everything”


the unit (per 100 mm, per 100,000)
a bare coefficient

title: Session 5 — Reporting and Extensions
text:
A counterfactual

fogged <- dg |> filter(fogging == "Yes"); cf <- fogged |> mutate(fogging = factor("No", levels = levels(dg$fogging)))
c(with_fogging = round(sum(predict(m_nb, newdata = fogged, type = "response"))), without_fogging = round(sum(predict(m_nb, newdata = cf, type = "response"))))

   with_fogging without_fogging 
           1363            2072 



Predict the expected cases as if fogging had not been done, and compare with what the model expects with it
About 700 cases averted (roughly a third), under the model’s assumptions
Give an interval (bootstrap or simulation) in a paper
It is only as good as the adjustment: unmeasured confounding remains

title: Session 5 — Reporting and Extensions
text:
Poisson for prevalence ratios
In cross-sectional data with a common yes/no outcome, the odds ratio overstates the prevalence ratio (regression workshop, Session 5). Poisson regression with robust SEs estimates the prevalence ratio directly:

pr <- glm(I(cases > 0) ~ fogging + slum, family = poisson, data = dg)
round(exp(cbind(PR = coef(pr), confint.default(pr, vcov. = vcovCL(pr, cluster = dg$ward)))), 2)

              PR 2.5 % 97.5 %
(Intercept) 0.78  0.71   0.86
foggingYes  0.95  0.79   1.14
slumSlum    1.08  0.94   1.23



family = poisson on a 0/1 outcome (no offset), with robust (sandwich) SEs
The alternatives are a log-binomial model (can fail to converge) or converting an OR with the baseline risk

title: Session 5 — Reporting and Extensions
text:
Beyond this workshop

Mixed models with a random effect for ward (glmmTMB, lme4)
Spatial and temporal dependence (neighbouring wards, lagged cases)
Distributed-lag models for rainfall and temperature
Interrupted time series for an intervention at a known date
Outbreak detection (Farrington, EARS) for surveillance

title: Session 5 — Reporting and Extensions
text:
Reporting checklist


Event, unit, period, denominator; number of events and units
Distribution: dispersion, zeros, and the model chosen and why
Rate ratios with 95% CI, the offset, the unit of each predictor
Adjustment set and how season/trend were handled
Clustering: robust or random-effect handling
Checks: fit over time, autocorrelation, sensitivity to Poisson/NB/zero-inflated
Limitations: reporting changes, ecological design, association not cause

Self-check quiz (1/5)

A negative binomial model gives a rate ratio of 0.66 for fogging. Which wording is best?

title: Session 5 — Reporting and Extensions
text:
Self-check quiz (2/5)

How are cases averted estimated from a count model?

Predict expected cases with and without the exposure; take the difference
Subtract observed cases in unfogged wards from fogged wards
Multiply the rate ratio by the number of wards in the study
Divide the total number of cases by the fogged months

title: Session 5 — Reporting and Extensions
text:
Self-check quiz (3/5)

When is Poisson regression with robust standard errors useful for a yes/no outcome?

To estimate a prevalence ratio when the outcome is common
To estimate an odds ratio for an outcome that is rare
To avoid having to code the outcome as a 0/1 variable
To model the time that passes until the event occurs

title: Session 5 — Reporting and Extensions
text:
Self-check quiz (4/5)

Which statement belongs in the limitations of the dengue analysis?

Reporting changed over time, and ward-level data cannot show individual effects
The model has too many wards for its results to be interpreted
Rate ratios cannot be calculated when the outcome is a count
The negative binomial distribution applies only to people, not wards

title: Session 3 — Overdispersion
text:
Where we are

Session 2: Poisson regression and rate ratios
Today: when the data are more variable than a Poisson allows, which is usual
By the end you can:

measure overdispersion
choose between quasi-Poisson, negative binomial and robust SEs
see why standard errors, not estimates, are the problem

title: Session 3 — Overdispersion
text:
The dispersion statistic

dispersion = sum of squared Pearson residuals / residual df (about 1 if Poisson fits)


m2 <- glm(cases ~ fogging + slum + rain_lag1 + month_index + sin(2 * pi * month / 12) + cos(2 * pi * month / 12) + offset(log(population)), family = poisson, data = dg)
sum(residuals(m2, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(m2)

[1] 7.938899



check_overdispersion(m2)

# Overdispersion test

       dispersion ratio =    7.939
  Pearson's Chi-Squared = 8518.439
                p-value =  < 0.001

title: Session 3 — Overdispersion
text:
What dispersion means

A dispersion of 7.9 means the Poisson standard errors are too small by about its square root (2.8 times). The coefficients are still reasonable; the p-values and CIs are not.

title: Session 3 — Overdispersion
text:
Why is count data overdispersed?

Unmeasured heterogeneity: wards differ in ways we did not record
Clustering: events cluster in space and time (outbreaks)
Contagion: one case causes others (not independent)
Zero inflation (Session 4)

title: Session 3 — Overdispersion
text:
Quasi-Poisson

m_q <- glm(formula(m2), family = quasipoisson, data = dg)
round(cbind(Poisson_SE = summary(m2)$coefficients[, 2], Quasi_SE = summary(m_q)$coefficients[, 2])[2:3, ], 3)

           Poisson_SE Quasi_SE
foggingYes      0.032    0.090
slumSlum        0.020    0.056


Same coefficients, standard errors multiplied by sqrt(dispersion). Simple; no AIC (not a full likelihood).

title: Session 3 — Overdispersion
text:
Negative binomial

m_nb <- MASS::glm.nb(formula(m2), data = dg)
c(theta = round(m_nb$theta, 2)); AIC(m2, m_nb)

theta 
  1.4 


     df       AIC
m2    7 10744.836
m_nb  8  5898.446



Var(Y) = mu + mu2 / theta


An extra parameter theta lets the variance grow faster than the mean; smaller theta = more overdispersion
A real likelihood: compare models by AIC
The usual first choice for overdispersed counts

title: Session 3 — Overdispersion
text:
Rate ratios compared

bind_rows(Poisson = tidy(m2, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE), NB = tidy(m_nb, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE), .id = "model") |>
  filter(term == "foggingYes") |> select(model, RR = estimate, low = conf.low, high = conf.high) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  model      RR   low  high
  <chr>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 Poisson  0.64  0.6   0.68
2 NB       0.66  0.54  0.8 



The point estimate barely moves; the CI is about three times wider with the negative binomial. Do not report the Poisson CI when the data are overdispersed.

title: Session 3 — Overdispersion
text:
Robust (clustered) standard errors

coeftest(m2, vcov = vcovCL(m2, cluster = dg$ward))[2:3, ]

             Estimate Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
foggingYes -0.4533550  0.1199850 -3.778432 0.0001578192
slumSlum    0.5362063  0.1688614  3.175423 0.0014961816



The same ward appears 36 times: observations are correlated
vcovCL(model, cluster = ward) gives cluster-robust standard errors, valid for correlated data
Use with Poisson (rates stay the same, SEs honest) or with NB

title: Session 1 — Counts, Rates and the Poisson Idea
section: A count is not a rate
text:
A count is not a rate

Count: how many events (cases)
Rate: events per unit of person-time at risk: cases / (people x time)
A ward of 60,000 will have more cases than a ward of 8,000 even at the same risk
Compare rates, not counts, unless you only want workload


c(cases = sum(dg$cases), rate_per_100k_person_months = round(sum(dg$cases) / sum(dg$population) * 1e5, 1))

                      cases rate_per_100k_person_months 
                    10411.0                        34.3 

dg |> group_by(slum) |> summarise(cases = sum(cases), person_months = sum(population), rate_per_100k = round(cases / person_months * 1e5, 1))

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  slum     cases person_months rate_per_100k
  <fct>    <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
1 Non-slum  4312      16516800          26.1

title: Session 1 — Counts, Rates and the Poisson Idea
text:
Person-time and the rate ratio

Person-time is the denominator: each ward-month contributes its population x 1 month. The slum rate ratio is about 1.7.

title: Session 1 — Counts, Rates and the Poisson Idea
text:
Counts of rare, independent events

P(Y = k) = e-mu muk / k! with mean = variance = mu


Events occur independently, at a constant rate, and one at a time
The single parameter mu is both the mean and the variance
Skewed for small mu, nearly symmetric for large mu
Poisson regression (Session 2) models log(mu) as a linear function of predictors


bind_rows(tibble(k = 0:25, p = dpois(0:25, 2), mu = "mean 2"), tibble(k = 0:25, p = dpois(0:25, 10), mu = "mean 10")) |>
  ggplot(aes(k, p, fill = mu)) + geom_col(position = "dodge") + labs(x = "Count", y = "Probability", fill = NULL)

title: Session 1 — Counts, Rates and the Poisson Idea
text: Counts of rare, independent events

title: Session 1 — Counts, Rates and the Poisson Idea
text:
Does our data look Poisson?

c(mean = round(mean(dg$cases), 1), variance = round(var(dg$cases), 0))

    mean variance 
     9.6    394.0 

c(observed_zeros = round(mean(dg$cases == 0), 3), poisson_expected_zeros = signif(dpois(0, mean(dg$cases)), 2))

        observed_zeros poisson_expected_zeros 
              0.202000               0.000065 



The variance is about 41 times the mean, and there are far more zeros than a Poisson allows. This is overdispersion (Session 3) and excess zeros (Session 4). Part of it is just different wards, seasons and rates mixed together, which regression can explain.

title: Session 1 — Counts, Rates and the Poisson Idea
text:
Trend and seasonality

dg |> group_by(date) |> summarise(cases = sum(cases)) |> ggplot(aes(date, cases)) + geom_line(colour = col_navy) + geom_point() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Cases in the city per month")



A clear monsoon peak every year, and a mild upward drift
Model it: month (sine and cosine, or factor(month)) and a time trend
Ignoring season confounds comparisons: fogging started in month 25, after growth

title: Session 5 — Assumptions and Reporting
text:
Where we are

Session 4: the Cox model and hazard ratios
Today: can we trust a single hazard ratio?
By the end you can:

test and plot the proportional-hazards assumption
fix a violation by stratifying or splitting time
judge whether censoring is acceptable
report a survival analysis

title: Session 5 — Assumptions and Reporting
text:
The assumption

The Cox model assumes the hazard ratio is constant over time. If one group is worse early and the same later, a single HR averages two different stories.


fit <- coxph(Surv(time_months, status) ~ age + sex + hiv + diabetes + smoker + bmi + mdr_tb + smear + treatment, data = tb)
zph <- cox.zph(fit)
round(zph$table, 3)

           chisq df     p
age        5.785  1 0.016
sex        0.008  1 0.928
hiv        0.276  1 0.600
diabetes   1.293  1 0.256
smoker     1.677  1 0.195
bmi        3.970  1 0.046
mdr_tb     0.022  1 0.881
smear     15.317  1 0.000
treatment  2.734  1 0.098
GLOBAL    30.465  9 0.000

title: Session 5 — Assumptions and Reporting
text:
Reading the test

cox.zph() tests whether Schoenfeld residuals trend with time, one p-value per term plus a global one
smear has a very small p-value: its effect changes over time
With nine terms tested, borderline p-values (age, BMI) can be chance: look at the plot before acting

title: Session 5 — Assumptions and Reporting
text:
Look at it

plot(zph[8]); abline(h = 0, col = "red")



A flat line means a constant log hazard ratio
Here the curve slopes down: strong effect early, little later
A second look: log-log plot of the curves; parallel lines support proportional hazards

title: Session 5 — Assumptions and Reporting
text: Look at it

title: Session 5 — Assumptions and Reporting
text:
Fix 1: stratify

cox_strat <- coxph(Surv(time_months, status) ~ age + sex + hiv + diabetes + smoker + bmi + mdr_tb + treatment + strata(smear), data = tb)
round(exp(coef(cox_strat)), 2)

         age      sexMale  hivPositive  diabetesYes    smokerYes          bmi 
        1.02         1.07         2.01         1.33         1.10         0.91 
   mdr_tbYes treatmentDOT 
        2.36         0.57 



strata(smear): a separate baseline hazard for each group, so the other HRs are not distorted
You lose an HR for smear itself, which is a reasonable price if smear is only a nuisance variable
Use for a categorical variable

title: Session 5 — Assumptions and Reporting
section: Fix 2: split time and estimate the effect in each period
text:
Fix 2: split time and estimate the effect in each period

tb_split <- survSplit(Surv(time_months, status) ~ ., data = tb, cut = 6, episode = "period")
tb_split$smear_pos <- as.numeric(tb_split$smear == "Positive")
cox_split <- coxph(Surv(tstart, time_months, status) ~ age + sex + hiv + diabetes + smoker + bmi + mdr_tb + treatment + smear_pos:factor(period), data = tb_split)
round(exp(coef(cox_split))[c("smear_pos:factor(period)1", "smear_pos:factor(period)2")], 2)

smear_pos:factor(period)1 smear_pos:factor(period)2 
                     3.28                      0.58 



“Smear-positive disease tripled the hazard in the first 6 months (HR about 3) and was not harmful afterwards (HR about 0.6).” The effect of time is itself a finding. Other options: time-varying covariates, landmark analysis, parametric models.

title: Session 5 — Assumptions and Reporting
text:
Is censoring “non-informative”?

Kaplan-Meier and Cox assume patients censored at time t have the same future risk as those who remain
If the sickest are lost to follow-up, the curve is too optimistic
Check: how many were lost, who (compare groups), and when
Sensitivity analysis: treat everyone lost as dead (worst case) and as alive (best case)


tb |> group_by(hiv) |> summarise(n = n(), pct_lost = round(100 * mean(censor_reason %in% "Lost to follow-up"), 1))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  hiv          n pct_lost
  <fct>    <int>    <dbl>
1 Negative   537     17.3
2 Positive    63     15.9

title: Session 5 — Assumptions and Reporting
text:
Other threats







Problem
What to do




Competing risks (death from another cause stops the event of interest)
cumulative incidence (tidycmprsk), Fine-Gray model; beyond this workshop


Immortal time bias (time before exposure counted as exposed)
define time zero carefully; time-varying exposure


Different time zero for groups
use the same starting point (e.g. start of treatment)


Too many covariates for the events
fewer predictors; shrinkage

title: Session 5 — Assumptions and Reporting
text:
Reporting checklist


Population, time zero, event, end of follow-up; number of patients, events, censored
Median follow-up (reverse KM) and reasons for censoring
Kaplan-Meier curves with number at risk; survival at fixed times with CI
Cox model: crude and adjusted HRs with CI, reference groups, units
Proportional-hazards check and what you did about violations
Limitations: informative censoring, competing risks, confounding, association, not cause

title: Session 3 — Comparing Survival: the Log-Rank Test
text:
Where we are

Session 2: Kaplan-Meier curves by group
Today: are the curves different beyond chance?
By the end you can:

run and read a log-rank test
use observed vs expected deaths to give the direction
stratify a log-rank test
explain why a t-test of follow-up time is wrong

title: Session 3 — Comparing Survival: the Log-Rank Test
text:
What it compares
At every event time, given how many are at risk in each group, how many deaths would we expect in each group if the curves were the same? The test adds up (observed − expected) over all event times.

H₀: the survival curves (hazards) are the same in all groups. Small p: evidence of a difference somewhere along follow-up. It uses the whole curve, and is most powerful when the hazards are proportional.

title: Session 3 — Comparing Survival: the Log-Rank Test
text:
HIV status

lr_hiv <- survdiff(Surv(time_months, status) ~ hiv, data = tb)
lr_hiv

Call:
survdiff(formula = Surv(time_months, status) ~ hiv, data = tb)

               N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
hiv=Negative 537       94    101.6     0.565       5.6
hiv=Positive  63       19     11.4     5.022       5.6

 Chisq= 5.6  on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.02 



Observed vs expected deaths: HIV-positive patients had more deaths than expected (19 vs 11.4)
Chisq on 1 df and its p-value: here p = 0.018
The test gives no size of effect: use the hazard ratio (Session 4)

title: Session 3 — Comparing Survival: the Log-Rank Test
text:
A null result

lr_sex <- survdiff(Surv(time_months, status) ~ sex, data = tb)
c(chisq = round(lr_sex$chisq, 2), p = round(1 - pchisq(lr_sex$chisq, 1), 2))

chisq     p 
 0.23  0.63 



p = 0.63 means no evidence of a difference by sex, not proof of none: look at the CI of the hazard ratio to see which differences remain plausible.

title: Session 3 — Comparing Survival: the Log-Rank Test
text:
Stratified log-rank
Compare HIV groups within treatment arms, then combine:

survdiff(Surv(time_months, status) ~ hiv + strata(treatment), data = tb)

Call:
survdiff(formula = Surv(time_months, status) ~ hiv + strata(treatment), 
    data = tb)

               N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
hiv=Negative 537       94    102.1     0.639      6.64
hiv=Positive  63       19     10.9     5.966      6.64

 Chisq= 6.6  on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.01 



Use when another variable also affects survival and is unbalanced between the groups
It cannot compare the stratifying variable itself, and adjusts for one factor at a time: for several, use Cox

title: Session 3 — Comparing Survival: the Log-Rank Test
text:
More than two groups

tb |> mutate(group = case_when(mdr_tb == "Yes" ~ "MDR-TB", hiv == "Positive" ~ "HIV, drug-sensitive", TRUE ~ "Drug-sensitive, HIV-negative")) |>
  survdiff(Surv(time_months, status) ~ group, data = _)

Call:
survdiff(formula = Surv(time_months, status) ~ group, data = mutate(tb, 
    group = case_when(mdr_tb == "Yes" ~ "MDR-TB", hiv == "Positive" ~ 
        "HIV, drug-sensitive", TRUE ~ "Drug-sensitive, HIV-negative")))

                                     N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
group=Drug-sensitive, HIV-negative 484       78    92.03      2.14     11.56
group=HIV, drug-sensitive           61       18    11.26      4.04      4.49
group=MDR-TB                        55       17     9.71      5.48      6.01

 Chisq= 11.7  on 2 degrees of freedom, p= 0.003 


An overall test on k groups has k − 1 df; it says some group differs. Follow with pairwise comparisons, adjusted for multiple testing.

title: Session 3 — Comparing Survival: the Log-Rank Test
text:
The wrong tests


t-test or Wilcoxon on follow-up time: mixes deaths and censored times, and answers a different question
Chi-square on “died yes/no” ignores follow-up time, which differs between patients



c(t_test = signif(t.test(time_months ~ hiv, data = tb)$p.value, 2), log_rank = signif(1 - pchisq(lr_hiv$chisq, 1), 2))

  t_test log_rank 
   0.300    0.018

title: Session 3 — Comparing Survival: the Log-Rank Test
text:
The log-rank test does not

Adjust for several covariates: use Cox regression
Give an effect size: report the hazard ratio with a CI
Work well when the curves cross: then the “average” difference can be near zero while the curves differ early and late

observed vs expected, the p-value from the chi-square
strata() and the wrong t-test


Time: 30 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments

title: Session 3 — Comparing Survival: the Log-Rank Test
text:
Self-check quiz (1/5)

What is the null hypothesis of the log-rank test comparing two groups?

The median survival time is the same in both groups
The numbers of patients at the start are equal in both groups
The survival curves are the same in both groups
The hazard ratio is exactly 1 at one particular time

title: Session 3 — Comparing Survival: the Log-Rank Test
text:
Self-check quiz (2/5)

HIV-positive patients had 19 observed deaths and 11.4 expected. How should this be read?

Fewer deaths than expected if survival were the same in both groups
More deaths than expected if survival were the same in both groups
The test has failed, because the two numbers are different
A difference of 7.6 deaths per 100 person-years

title: Session 3 — Comparing Survival: the Log-Rank Test
text:
Self-check quiz (3/5)

Why is a t-test on the follow-up time of two groups inappropriate for survival data?

The t-test needs both of the groups to have the same number of patients
Follow-up times follow a normal distribution in a typical sample of patients
Follow-up times mix deaths and censored times, so it asks the wrong question
A t-test can be used for yes/no outcomes and not for times to an event

title: Session 3 — Comparing Survival: the Log-Rank Test
text:
Self-check quiz (4/5)

The log-rank test by sex gives p = 0.63. Which conclusion is best?

Men and women have been shown to have identical survival in the cohort
Sex has no effect on survival in any population of TB patients
The test was underpowered, so it should be repeated on more patients
No evidence of a difference in survival by sex in this cohort

title: Session 3 — Comparing Survival: the Log-Rank Test
text:
Self-check quiz (5/5)

When is a stratified log-rank test most useful?

When another factor affects survival and is unbalanced between groups
When the survival curves of the two groups cross over each other once
When there are no deaths recorded in one of the two groups compared
When the follow-up times of the patients are normally distributed

title: Session 3 — Comparing Survival: the Log-Rank Test
text:
Score and take-home
Your score: 

Log-rank: compares the whole curves; H₀ = same survival
Observed vs expected deaths give the direction
Stratify for one other factor; use Cox for several
Never t-test follow-up times; a non-significant p is not proof of no difference

Next: Session 4: Cox regression

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
text:
Where we are

Regression workshop: outcomes that are a measurement or a yes/no
Today: the outcome is how long until something happens: death, relapse, recovery, default from treatment
By the end you can:

say what censoring is, and why you cannot drop or average censored patients
define survival, hazard and cumulative incidence
build a Surv object and compute person-time and an incidence rate
describe follow-up correctly

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
section: Our data: a synthetic TB cohort
text:
Our data: a synthetic TB cohort



600 adults starting TB treatment, followed for up to 24 months
Outcome: death; time_months and status (1 = died, 0 = censored)
Predictors: age, sex, HIV, diabetes, smoking, BMI, MDR-TB, smear status, DOT (supervised treatment)
Invented, but built to behave like a real cohort



tb |> select(id, age, hiv, mdr_tb, treatment, time_months, status) |> head(6)

# A tibble: 6 × 7
  id      age hiv      mdr_tb treatment         time_months status
  <chr> <dbl> <fct>    <fct>  <fct>                   <dbl>  <dbl>
1 TB001    43 Negative No     Self-administered         7.8      0
2 TB002    46 Negative No     DOT                      15.2      0
3 TB003    15 Negative No     DOT                      23.8      0
4 TB004    69 Negative No     Self-administered         2.6      0
5 TB005    73 Negative No     DOT                      20.7      0
6 TB006    42 Negative No     DOT                      19.9      0

table(tb$status)


  0   1 
487 113

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
text:
Two problems with ordinary methods

Different follow-up: a patient enrolled last month has had little time to die; one enrolled two years ago has had a lot. Comparing proportions who died ignores this
Censoring: for many patients we do not observe the event


Censored = we know the patient was alive at least until their last contact, but not what happened afterwards.








Why censored
Example




Administrative
still alive when the study ended


Lost to follow-up
moved away, stopped attending


Competing event
died of something else (a different question; see Session 5)

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
text:
Censored patients still carry information

tb |> slice(1:15) |> mutate(row = row_number(), outcome = ifelse(status == 1, "Died", "Censored")) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = reorder(id, -row))) + geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = time_months, yend = reorder(id, -row)), colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(x = time_months, colour = outcome, shape = outcome), size = 3) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(Died = col_red, Censored = col_blue)) +
  labs(x = "Months of follow-up", y = NULL, colour = NULL, shape = NULL)



Each line is one patient; a dot at the end marks death or censoring
A censored patient contributes their time at risk up to the last contact
Dropping them wastes information and biases towards early deaths; treating them as survivors forever biases the other way

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
text: Censored patients still carry information

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
text:
The three quantities







Quantity
Meaning




Survival S(t)
probability of being alive beyond time t


Hazard h(t)
the instantaneous rate of dying at t, among those still alive


Cumulative incidence
1 − S(t): the probability of having died by t




The hazard is a rate (events per person-time), not a probability. Cox regression (Session 4) models the hazard.

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
text:
Time and event together

y <- Surv(tb$time_months, tb$status)
head(y, 10)

 [1]  7.8+ 15.2+ 23.8+  2.6+ 20.7+ 19.9+  3.8+ 19.4+ 14.9+ 17.7+



Surv(time, event) pairs each follow-up time with its event indicator
A + after a time marks a censored observation (still alive at least that long)
Check the coding: 1 = event, 0 = censored (factor and TRUE/FALSE also work, but check!)
This object goes on the left of every survival model: survfit(Surv(...) ~ group), coxph(Surv(...) ~ x)

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
section: Do not summarise survival times with a mean
text:
Do not summarise survival times with a mean

c(mean_all = mean(tb$time_months), mean_among_deaths = mean(tb$time_months[tb$status == 1]))

         mean_all mean_among_deaths 
        14.873500          5.780531 



Neither number is a survival time. The first mixes deaths and censored times; the second looks only at those who died and ignores everyone who survived, so it is biased downwards.

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
text:
Incidence rate

py <- sum(tb$time_months) / 12
c(deaths = sum(tb$status), person_years = round(py, 1), rate_per_100_py = round(sum(tb$status) / py * 100, 1))

         deaths    person_years rate_per_100_py 
          113.0           743.7            15.2 



Rate = events / person-time at risk (here per 100 person-years)
It uses everyone’s time, censored or not
Valid if the hazard is roughly constant; Kaplan-Meier (Session 2) removes that assumption

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
text:
Describing follow-up honestly

rkm <- survfit(Surv(time_months, 1 - status) ~ 1, data = tb)
c(median_raw_time = median(tb$time_months), median_followup_reverse_KM = unname(summary(rkm)$table["median"]))

           median_raw_time median_followup_reverse_KM 
                      16.7                       18.1 



The reverse Kaplan-Meier swaps the roles of event and censoring, so it asks “how long would a typical patient be followed if they did not die?”. The median of the raw times is pulled down by deaths and understates follow-up.

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
text:
Checklist before any analysis


Define time zero (start of treatment, diagnosis) and the event precisely
Check time is positive and in one unit; status is coded 0/1
Count events and censored; tabulate why censored
Report median follow-up (reverse KM), person-time and events

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
text:
🔧 Switch to R — Lab 1

File: survival-workshop/labs/lab1_data.R

table() of status and censoring reasons
Surv(): the + marks censored times
person-years, a rate per 100 person-years, reverse Kaplan-Meier


Time: 30 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
text:
Self-check quiz (1/5)

What does a patient who was alive at the last clinic visit (month 17) and then moved away contribute to the analysis?

Nothing, since the outcome for this patient is unknown
A death at month 17, since no later contact exists
Their 17 months at risk, as a censored observation
An observation that must be treated as survival forever

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
text:
Self-check quiz (2/5)

A TB cohort has 113 deaths among 600 patients. Why is ‘mortality = 113/600 = 19%’ a weak summary?

The number of deaths is too small to be divided by 600 patients, so it is unstable
Patients differ in follow-up, so a proportion mixes unequal time at risk
Mortality is reported as a count and should not be given as a percentage
The 19% ignores the fact that some of the patients in the cohort were female

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
text:
Self-check quiz (3/5)

In the output of a Surv object, 17.2+ means what?

The patient died at 17.2 months
The patient survived exactly 17.2 months in total
The patient was censored at 17.2 months
The patient had a second event after 17.2 months

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
text:
Self-check quiz (4/5)

What is the hazard in survival analysis?

The probability of surviving beyond a given time point in the cohort
The total number of deaths divided by the total number of patients
The median time until the event occurs for half of the patients
The instantaneous event rate among those still event-free

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
text:
Self-check quiz (5/5)

Why is the reverse Kaplan-Meier median a better description of follow-up than the median of the raw follow-up times?

Deaths shorten raw times, so their median understates follow-up
The reverse method removes all of the patients who were censored
Raw follow-up times cannot be calculated when some patients died
The reverse method gives the median survival time of the patients

title: Session 1 — Time-to-Event Data
text:
Score and take-home
Your score: 

Censoring: observed up to a time, then unknown; keep these patients
Survival S(t), hazard h(t), cumulative incidence 1 − S(t)
Surv(time, event): a + means censored
Use person-time rates, not a mean of follow-up times; report median follow-up by reverse KM

Next: Session 2: Kaplan-Meier curves

title: Quarto — Publication
text:
Journal-Quality Documents
A well-structured YAML for a manuscript-style document:
---
title: "Effect of Clean Fuel Intervention on Blood Pressure: A Community Trial"
author:
  - name: "Dr. Mukul Maheshwari"
    affiliation: "Department of Community Medicine"
    email: "author@institution.ac.in"
  - name: "Dr. Rudresh Negi"
    affiliation: "Department of Community Medicine"
date: today
abstract: |
  **Background:** Indoor air pollution remains a major public health concern...
  **Methods:** A cluster-randomised trial was conducted...
  **Results:** ...
  **Conclusion:** ...
keywords: [indoor air pollution, blood pressure, community trial, R]
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
    number-sections: true
    theme: flatly
  pdf:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
    cite-method: biblatex
    pdf-engine: xelatex
    mainfont: "Times New Roman"
    fontsize: 12pt
    geometry: "margin=2.5cm"
bibliography: references.bib
csl: vancouver.csl          # citation style (download from Zotero CSL repo)
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
---

title: Quarto — Publication
Quarto — Publication
text:
Callout Blocks
Callouts draw attention to key information without disrupting text flow.
::: {.callout-note}
This is a note — useful for clarifications and asides.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}

title: Quarto — Publication
text:
Multi-File Quarto Projects

Books
A Quarto book renders multiple .qmd files into a single structured document (HTML, PDF, or ePub).
my-book/
├── _quarto.yml
├── index.qmd        (preface / front matter)
├── 01-intro.qmd
├── 02-methods.qmd
├── 03-results.qmd
├── 04-discussion.qmd
└── references.qmd
_quarto.yml for a book:
project:
  type: book

book:
  title: "Community Trial Methods in R"
  author: "Dr. Mukul Maheshwari"
  date: today
  chapters:
    - index.qmd
    - 01-intro.qmd
    - 02-methods.qmd
    - 03-results.qmd
    - 04-discussion.qmd
    - references.qmd

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
  pdf:
    documentclass: scrbook


Websites
For a multi-page website (like this workshop), see the project’s _quarto.yml for a working example of navbar configuration, profiles, and output directories.

title: Quarto — Publication
text:
GitHub + Quarto Publishing Workflow

Option A — Push rendered HTML to GitHub Pages

Render your project locally: quarto render
Output goes to docs/ (set output-dir: docs in _quarto.yml)
Commit and push the docs/ folder to GitHub
In your repository: Settings → Pages → Source → Branch: main, Folder: /docs

# Full publish cycle
quarto render
git add docs/
git commit -m "Rebuild site"
git push


Option B — GitHub Actions (automated rebuild)
Create .github/workflows/publish.yml:
name: Publish Quarto Site

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2
        with:
          packages: |
            any::quarto
            any::tidyverse
            any::ggstatsplot
            any::gtsummary

      - uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2

      - name: Render and publish
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2
        with:
          target: gh-pages
With this workflow, every push to main automatically rebuilds and deploys the site.


Option C — Quarto Pub (zero configuration)
quarto publish quarto-pub
Creates a free public site at username.quarto.pub/project-name. Suitable for sharing documents without managing a GitHub repository.

title: Quarto — Publication
text:
Embedding Shiny in Quarto
For lightweight interactivity within a static Quarto document.

Using shinylive (no server required)
shinylive compiles Shiny to WebAssembly — no Shiny server needed.
---
title: "Interactive Report"
format: html
filters:
  - shinylive
---
```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
library(shiny)
library(ggplot2)

ui <- fluidPage(
  sliderInput("bins", "Bins:", 5, 50, 20),
  plotOutput("hist")
)

server <- function(input, output) {
  output$hist <- renderPlot({
    ggplot(data.frame(x = rnorm(500)), aes(x)) +
      geom_histogram(bins = input$bins)
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```
Install shinylive:
install.packages("shinylive")
quarto::quarto_add_extension("quarto-ext/shinylive")


Embedding a deployed Shiny app with <iframe>
If you have an app on shinyapps.io:
<iframe src="https://yourname.shinyapps.io/yourapp/"
        width="100%" height="600px"
        style="border: none;">
</iframe>

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
Note

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
Functions covered in this module



Function
Use case




ggwithinstats()
Repeated measures / paired comparisons


ggbarstats()
Proportions across categorical groups


ggpiestats()
Proportions as pie / donut charts


Customising appearance
Colours, themes, subtitle text


Interpreting Bayes factors
Introduction

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
ggwithinstats() — Repeated Measures
Use this when the same participants are measured more than once (paired/within-subjects design) — for example, pre-post measurements.

library(ggstatsplot)
library(tidyr)

# Reshape from wide to long for within-subjects comparison
overall_long <- overall_up |>
  select(member_id, sbp_0m, sbp_3m) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(sbp_0m, sbp_3m),
    names_to  = "timepoint",
    values_to = "sbp"
  ) |>
  mutate(timepoint = factor(timepoint,
                            levels = c("sbp_0m", "sbp_3m"),
                            labels = c("Baseline", "3 Months")))

ggwithinstats(
  data    = overall_long,
  x       = timepoint,
  y       = sbp,
  subject.id = member_id,       # links pairs across timepoints
  title   = "Systolic BP: Baseline vs 3 Months"
)

Key differences from ggbetweenstats():

subject.id is required — it tells the function which rows are paired
Uses a paired t-test (parametric) or Wilcoxon signed-rank (non-parametric)
Lines connect paired observations in the plot

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
ggbarstats() — Proportions
Use this when you want to compare proportions of a categorical outcome across groups. The output includes a χ² or Fisher’s exact test.

ggbarstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,           # grouping variable (x-axis)
  y     = tobacco_type,        # outcome category (fill)
  title = "Tobacco Type by Fuel Type"
)

What the output shows:

Stacked bar chart with proportion labels
χ² test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and Cramér’s V effect size
Pairwise comparisons between bars (if > 2 groups)

Swap axes to change orientation:

# Make tobacco_type the grouping variable
ggbarstats(data = overall_up, x = tobacco_type, y = fuel_type)

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
ggpiestats() — Pie / Donut Charts
Use this for a single categorical variable, or two categorical variables where a pie chart is appropriate for the audience.

# Single variable — proportions of intervention types
ggpiestats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = intervention,
  title = "Distribution of Intervention Groups"
)


# Two variables — tobacco type by intervention
ggpiestats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = tobacco_type,
  y     = intervention,       # creates faceted pies
  title = "Tobacco Type by Intervention"
)







WarningWhen to use pie charts



Pie charts are appropriate when there are ≤ 5 categories and the audience is non-technical. For more categories or detailed comparisons, prefer ggbarstats().

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
Customising appearance
All ggstatsplot functions return a ggplot2 object, so you can extend them normally.

library(ggplot2)

ggbetweenstats(
  data        = overall_up,
  x           = fuel_type,
  y           = sbp_0m,
  # Colours for each group
  palette     = "Set2",
  package     = "RColorBrewer",
  # Remove the subtitle (statistical results) if preferred
  results.subtitle = TRUE,
  # Change point size and transparency
  point.args  = list(size = 2, alpha = 0.4),
  title       = "Systolic BP by Fuel Type"
) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  labs(caption = "Source: NCTOH Study Dataset")

Common customisation parameters:



Parameter
What it controls




palette + package
Colour palette for groups


results.subtitle
Show/hide statistical annotation


point.args
Size, alpha, shape of data points


centrality.plotting
Show/hide mean/median marker


xlab / ylab
Axis labels

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
Introduction to Bayes Factors
When you set type = "bayes", ggstatsplot reports a Bayes Factor (BF₁₀) instead of a p-value.

ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  type  = "bayes",
  title = "Systolic BP by Fuel Type (Bayesian)"
)

Interpreting BF₁₀:



BF₁₀
Interpretation




> 100
Extreme evidence for H₁


30–100
Very strong evidence for H₁


10–30
Strong evidence for H₁


3–10
Moderate evidence for H₁


1–3
Anecdotal evidence for H₁


~1
No evidence either way


1/3–1
Anecdotal evidence for H₀


< 1/10
Strong–extreme evidence for H₀




BF₁₀ > 3: reasonably confident that H₁ (an effect exists) is supported
BF₁₀ < 1/3: reasonably confident that H₀ (no effect) is supported
Values between 1/3 and 3 are inconclusive







Note



Bayesian inference and deeper interpretation of Bayes factors is covered in ggstatsplot — Advanced.

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
Bayesian Reporting Workflow
The Bayesian approach in ggstatsplot uses the BayesFactor package internally. The goal is to quantify how much evidence exists for or against an effect, rather than simply crossing a significance threshold.

Setting priors

library(ggstatsplot)

# Default Cauchy prior (r = 0.707) — appropriate for most comparisons
ggbetweenstats(
  data         = overall_up,
  x            = intervention,
  y            = sbp_0m,
  type         = "bayes",
  bf.prior     = 0.707,        # scale of Cauchy prior on effect size
  title        = "SBP by Intervention (Bayesian, default prior)"
)

# Narrow prior — use if you expect a small effect
ggbetweenstats(
  data         = overall_up,
  x            = intervention,
  y            = sbp_0m,
  type         = "bayes",
  bf.prior     = 0.5,
  title        = "SBP by Intervention (narrow prior)"
)



Reporting Bayes factors in text
When BF₁₀ = 18.4:

“A Bayesian independent-samples t-test revealed moderate-to-strong evidence for a difference in baseline SBP between intervention groups, BF₁₀ = 18.4, δ = 0.41, 95% credible interval [0.18, 0.65].”

When BF₁₀ = 0.21:

“A Bayesian independent-samples t-test provided moderate evidence in favour of the null hypothesis (no difference in SBP), BF₁₀ = 0.21.”







TipKey distinction: BF₁₀ vs BF₀₁




BF₁₀: evidence for H₁ over H₀ (use when testing for an effect)
BF₀₁ = 1/BF₁₀: evidence for H₀ over H₁ (use when supporting the null)

ggstatsplot reports BF₁₀ by default. To interpret support for H₀, invert it.

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
grouped_* Functions — Faceted Comparisons
The grouped_* variants run the same comparison separately within each level of a grouping variable and combine the results into a faceted plot.

# Compare SBP across tobacco types, separately by sex
grouped_ggbetweenstats(
  data             = overall_up,
  x                = tobacco_type,
  y                = sbp_0m,
  grouping.var     = sex,           # one panel per sex
  title            = "SBP by Tobacco Type, stratified by Sex",
  plotgrid.args    = list(ncol = 2)
)


# Correlation stratified by intervention group
grouped_ggscatterstats(
  data         = overall_up,
  x            = current_age,
  y            = sbp_0m,
  grouping.var = intervention,
  title        = "Age vs SBP by Intervention Group"
)

Available grouped functions:

grouped_ggbetweenstats()
grouped_ggwithinstats()
grouped_ggscatterstats()
grouped_gghistostats()
grouped_ggbarstats()
grouped_ggpiestats()
grouped_ggcorrmat()
grouped_ggdotplotstats()

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
ggcorrmat() — Correlation Matrix
Visualises pairwise correlations across multiple continuous variables with significance annotations.

ggcorrmat(
  data   = overall_up |> select(current_age, sbp_0m, sbp_3m, sbp_6m,
                                 consumption_per_day_0m),
  title  = "Correlation Matrix — Baseline Variables",
  type   = "parametric"     # "parametric", "nonparametric", "robust", "bayes"
)

Choosing the correlation type:



type
Method
When to use




"parametric"
Pearson’s r
Continuous, approximately normal


"nonparametric"
Spearman’s ρ
Ordinal or skewed distributions


"robust"
Percentage bend r
Presence of outliers


"bayes"
Bayesian r
Quantify evidence, not just significance

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
Combining with patchwork
All ggstatsplot outputs are ggplot2 objects and compose naturally with patchwork.

library(patchwork)

p1 <- ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = intervention,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  title = "Baseline SBP"
)

p2 <- ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = intervention,
  y     = sbp_3m,
  title = "3-Month SBP"
)

p3 <- ggscatterstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = sbp_0m,
  y     = sbp_3m,
  title = "Baseline vs 3-Month SBP"
)

# Compose: two plots on top, one full-width below
(p1 | p2) / p3 +
  plot_annotation(
    title   = "Blood Pressure Outcomes by Intervention",
    caption = "Source: NCTOH Study Dataset"
  )

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
Publication-ready output

library(ggplot2)

pub_plot <- ggbetweenstats(
  data             = overall_up,
  x                = intervention,
  y                = sbp_0m,
  type             = "parametric",
  pairwise.display = "significant",    # show only significant comparisons
  p.adjust.method  = "bonferroni",
  title            = "Baseline Systolic Blood Pressure by Intervention Group",
  xlab             = "Intervention Group",
  ylab             = "Systolic BP (mmHg)",
  package          = "RColorBrewer",
  palette          = "Set1"
) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.line        = element_line(linewidth = 0.5),
    plot.caption     = element_text(hjust = 0, colour = "grey50")
  ) +
  labs(caption = "Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons shown for p < 0.05")

# Save at print quality
ggsave("figures/sbp_by_intervention.png",
       pub_plot, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300)

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
Case Study: Healthcare Data
A complete example using the NCTOH study dataset — comparing the change in SBP across intervention groups, accounting for tobacco type.

library(ggstatsplot)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)

# Derive SBP change variable
study_data <- overall_up |>
  mutate(sbp_change = sbp_3m - sbp_0m)

# 1. Overall change by intervention
p_overall <- ggbetweenstats(
  data  = study_data,
  x     = intervention,
  y     = sbp_change,
  type  = "parametric",
  title = "Change in SBP at 3 Months"
)

# 2. Stratified by tobacco type
p_strat <- grouped_ggbetweenstats(
  data         = study_data,
  x            = intervention,
  y            = sbp_change,
  grouping.var = tobacco_type,
  title        = "SBP Change Stratified by Tobacco Type",
  plotgrid.args = list(ncol = 3)
)

# View each
p_overall
p_strat

title: Exporting plots
text: Exporting plots from R can be done in several ways, depending on the desired output format and quality. Here are some common methods to export plots:

title: Exporting plots
text:
Using R’s Built-in Functions
R provides several built-in functions for exporting plots to different formats:

Raster Formats

png(), jpeg(), tiff(), bmp(): These functions save plots in raster formats. You can specify filename, dimensions, and resolution.

# PNG format (good for web)
png("plot.png", width = 800, height = 600, res = 100)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

# High-resolution TIFF for publications
tiff("plot.tiff", width = 8, height = 6, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()


Vector Formats

pdf(): Saves plots in PDF format, vector-based and scalable.
svg(): Saves plots in SVG format, ideal for web and scalable graphics.

# PDF for high-quality prints
pdf("plot.pdf", width = 8, height = 6)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

# SVG for web use
svg("plot.svg", width = 8, height = 6)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

title: Exporting plots
text:
Exporting ggplot2 Plots
For ggplot2 plots, the ggsave() function is the most convenient way to export:
library(ggplot2)

# Create a plot
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point()

# Save in different formats
ggsave("plot.png", p, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 150)
ggsave("plot.pdf", p, width = 8, height = 6)
ggsave("plot.svg", p, width = 8, height = 6)

Controlling Output Quality

Resolution (DPI): Higher DPI for print quality (300+), lower for web (72-150)
Dimensions: Specify in inches or pixels
Aspect Ratio: Maintain proportions for consistency

# High-resolution for publications
ggsave("publication_plot.tiff", p, 
       width = 6, height = 4, 
       dpi = 300, 
       device = "tiff")

# Web-optimized PNG
ggsave("web_plot.png", p, 
       width = 800, height = 600, 
       dpi = 100, 
       units = "px")

title: Exporting plots
text:
Advanced Exporting Techniques

Exporting Multiple Plots
# Save multiple plots to PDF
pdf("multiple_plots.pdf")
plot1 <- ggplot(data1, aes(x, y)) + geom_point()
print(plot1)
plot2 <- ggplot(data2, aes(x, y)) + geom_line()
print(plot2)
dev.off()


Using Cairo for Better Quality
The Cairo graphics library can provide better quality for some formats:
install.packages("Cairo")
library(Cairo)

CairoPNG("high_quality.png", width = 800, height = 600)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()


Exporting to Clipboard
For quick sharing:
# Windows
savePlot("clipboard", type = "wmf")

# Or for ggplot2
ggsave("clipboard", p, device = "png")

title: Exporting plots
text:
Best Practices

Choose the right format: PDF/SVG for vector graphics, PNG/TIFF for raster
Set appropriate resolution: 300 DPI for print, 72-150 for screen
Consider file size: Vector formats scale better but may be larger
Test outputs: Always check exported files in target applications
Use consistent dimensions: Maintain aspect ratios across exports

title: Exporting plots
text:
Common Issues and Solutions

Plot not saving: Ensure dev.off() is called after plotting
Low quality: Increase DPI or use vector formats
Wrong dimensions: Specify units explicitly (inches, cm, pixels)
Colors not matching: Check color profiles and device settings

title: Advanced Exporting Techniques
text:
This chapter covers advanced techniques for exporting plots, including programmatic generation, batch processing, custom devices, and integration with other tools.




library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

# Create plots for each cylinder group
plots <- mtcars %>%
  split(.$cyl) %>%
  map(~ ggplot(.x, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + 
        geom_point() + 
        ggtitle(paste("Cylinders:", .x$cyl[1])))

# Save each plot
walk2(plots, names(plots), 
      ~ ggsave(filename = paste0("plot_cyl_", .x, ".png"), 
               plot = .y, 
               width = 6, height = 4))



# Generate timestamped filenames
timestamp <- format(Sys.time(), "%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")

ggsave(paste0("analysis_plot_", timestamp, ".pdf"), 
       plot = p, 
       width = 8, height = 6)






save_plot_multiple_formats <- function(plot, filename_base, 
                                     formats = c("png", "pdf", "svg")) {
  for (fmt in formats) {
    filename <- paste0(filename_base, ".", fmt)
    ggsave(filename, plot, width = 8, height = 6)
  }
}

# Usage
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
save_plot_multiple_formats(p, "mtcars_scatter")



datasets <- list(
  mtcars = mtcars,
  iris = iris,
  airquality = airquality
)

for (name in names(datasets)) {
  data <- datasets[[name]]
  # Create appropriate plot based on data
  if (name == "mtcars") {
    p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
  } else if (name == "iris") {
    p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width, color = Species)) + 
      geom_point()
  }
  
  ggsave(paste0(name, "_plot.png"), p, width = 6, height = 4)
}






library(Cairo)

# High-quality PNG
CairoPNG("high_quality.png", width = 800, height = 600, 
         bg = "white", pointsize = 12)
plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
dev.off()

# PDF with embedded fonts
CairoPDF("embedded_fonts.pdf", width = 8, height = 6, 
         family = "Arial")
plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
dev.off()



# Create a custom device wrapper
save_high_res <- function(filename, plot_func, ...) {
  png(filename, width = 1200, height = 800, res = 150, ...)
  plot_func()
  dev.off()
}

# Usage
my_plot <- function() {
  plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg, 
       xlab = "Weight", ylab = "MPG",
       main = "High Resolution Plot")
}

save_high_res("high_res_plot.png", my_plot)






library(tikzDevice)

# Export as TikZ for LaTeX
tikz("plot.tex", width = 4, height = 3)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
dev.off()



# Export as HTML with plotly
library(plotly)
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(ggplotly(p), "interactive_plot.html")






# Create publication-ready theme
publication_theme <- theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 12, family = "Times"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point() +
  publication_theme +
  labs(title = "Publication Quality Plot")

ggsave("publication_plot.pdf", p, 
       width = 6, height = 4, 
       device = cairo_pdf)



library(cowplot)

# Create individual plots
p1 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
p2 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) + geom_boxplot()
p3 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = hp)) + geom_histogram()

# Combine into single figure
combined <- plot_grid(p1, p2, p3, 
                      labels = c("A", "B", "C"),
                      ncol = 2)

# Save combined figure
ggsave("combined_figure.pdf", combined, 
       width = 10, height = 8)






# For large datasets, use sampling or aggregation
large_data <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100000), y = rnorm(100000))

# Option 1: Sample data
sample_data <- large_data[sample(nrow(large_data), 10000), ]
ggplot(sample_data, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.1)
ggsave("sampled_plot.png")

# Option 2: Use density plots
ggplot(large_data, aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  geom_density2d() +
  geom_point(data = sample_data, alpha = 0.1)
ggsave("density_plot.png")



# Clear graphics devices
graphics.off()

# Force garbage collection
gc()

# Monitor memory usage
library(pryr)
mem_used()






check_plot_quality <- function(filename) {
  # Check file exists
  if (!file.exists(filename)) {
    stop("File was not created")
  }
  
  # Check file size (basic quality indicator)
  size <- file.info(filename)$size
  if (size < 1000) {
    warning("File seems too small, may indicate error")
  }
  
  # For images, could check dimensions
  if (grepl("\\.png$", filename)) {
    img <- png::readPNG(filename)
    message("Image dimensions: ", dim(img)[1], "x", dim(img)[2])
  }
}

# Usage
ggsave("test_plot.png", ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point())
check_plot_quality("test_plot.png")





Automate repetitive tasks: Use functions and loops for batch processing
Standardize formats: Establish consistent dimensions and resolutions
Quality control: Implement checks for successful exports
Performance awareness: Optimize for large datasets
Version control: Track plot versions with timestamps or git
Documentation: Comment code for reproducible exports
Cross-platform compatibility: Test exports on target systems

text: Regression models describe and quantify the relationship between an outcome and one or more predictors. This module builds up in tiers — start with a single predictor, then add predictors, then move on to diagnostics and logistic regression.

title: Regression Analysis

Simple Linear Regression

  age = rnorm(100, 50, 10),
  blood_pressure = rnorm(100, 120, 15),
  treatment = sample(c("A", "B"), 100, replace = TRUE)
)

summary(model_simple)

title: Regression Analysis
text:
Regression Diagnostics
A fitted model is only trustworthy once its assumptions have been checked.

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model)









# Residuals vs fitted, and a normal Q-Q check
qqnorm(residuals(model))
qqline(residuals(model), col = "red")








Watch for: non-random patterns in residuals-vs-fitted (non-linearity), points far off the Q-Q line (non-normal residuals), and high-leverage points in the residuals-vs-leverage panel.

title: Regression Analysis
text:
Logistic Regression
When the outcome is binary rather than continuous, use glm() with a binomial family instead of lm().

data$outcome_bin <- ifelse(data$outcome == "Improved", 1, 0)

model_log <- glm(outcome_bin ~ age + treatment, data = data, family = binomial)
summary(model_log)

title: Regression Analysis
text:
Univariate Regression Screening
Before building a multivariable model, it’s common to screen each predictor on its own first. gtsummary::tbl_uvregression() fits one regression per predictor and lays the results out in a single comparison table.

data$bmi <- rnorm(100, 27, 4)

tbl_uvregression(
  data[, c("blood_pressure", "age", "treatment", "bmi")],
  method = lm,
  y = blood_pressure,
  hide_n = TRUE
)

title: Regression Analysis
text:
Cox Proportional Hazards Regression
For time-to-event outcomes (e.g. time to recovery, time to relapse), use survival::coxph() instead of lm()/glm(). It models the hazard of the event happening at any given time, adjusted for covariates.

library(survival)

data$time  <- rexp(100, rate = 0.05)
data$event <- rbinom(100, 1, 0.7)   # 1 = event observed, 0 = censored

cox_model <- coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ age + treatment, data = data)
summary(cox_model)

Call:

exponentiate = TRUE reports hazard ratios: above 1 means a faster time-to-event (higher instantaneous risk) as the predictor increases, below 1 means a slower one.

fit <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ treatment, data = data)
plot(
  fit, col = c("#3498db", "#e74c3c"), lwd = 2,
  xlab = "Time", ylab = "Survival probability",
  main = "Kaplan-Meier Curves by Treatment"
)
legend("topright", legend = c("Treatment A", "Treatment B"),
       col = c("#3498db", "#e74c3c"), lwd = 2)








The Kaplan-Meier curve shows the estimated probability of not yet having experienced the event over time for each treatment group — a purely descriptive view, independent of the Cox model’s covariate adjustment above.

title: Regression Analysis
text:
Model Diagnostics with performance
The performance package gives a quick, standardized diagnostic check for a fitted model, going further than the base-R diagnostic plots used earlier.

library(performance)

check_model(model)









r2(model)

# R2 for Linear Regression
       R2: 0.000
  adj. R2: -0.020

check_collinearity(model)

# Check for Multicollinearity

Low Correlation

      Term  VIF  VIF 95% CI adj. VIF Tolerance Tolerance 95% CI
       age 1.00 [1.00, Inf]     1.00      1.00     [0.00, 1.00]
 treatment 1.00 [1.00, Inf]     1.00      1.00     [0.00, 1.00]


check_model() bundles several checks — linearity, homogeneity of variance, normality of residuals, influential observations, and collinearity — into one panel. check_collinearity() reports Variance Inflation Factors (VIF) on their own; values above roughly 5 suggest predictors are too correlated with each other to interpret their individual coefficients reliably.

title: Practical Application
text:
Case Study 1: Publication Figure
Scenario: Need publication-ready figure for medical journal
Requirements: - High resolution (300 DPI) - Grayscale-friendly - Clear statistical annotations - Professional formatting

title: Practical Application
text:
Publication Figure - Code


Code
# Treatment effect with confidence intervals
model <- lm(SysBP_12m ~ TreatmentGroup + Age + BMI_0m + SysBP_0m,
           data = health_data)

library(ggeffects)
effects <- ggpredict(model, terms = "TreatmentGroup")

p <- plot(effects) +
  labs(title = "Treatment Effect on Systolic Blood Pressure",
       subtitle = "Adjusted for age, BMI, and baseline BP",
       x = "Treatment Group",
       y = "Predicted Systolic BP (mmHg)",
       caption = "Error bars: 95% confidence intervals. n=500 per group.") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none"
  )

# Save high-res
ggsave("figure1.tiff", p, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)
ggsave("figure1.eps", p, width = 7, height = 5, device = cairo_ps)
