title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4
text:
Setup


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readxl)
library(ggthemes)
library(paletteer)
library(patchwork)
# remotes::install_github("haleyjeppson/ggmosaic")
library(ggmosaic)  # For mosaic plots

# Load data with all transformations
bp_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx") %>%
  mutate(
    SysBP_Change = SysBP_6m - SysBP_0m,
    DiaBP_Change = DiaBP_6m - DiaBP_0m,
    AgeGroup = cut(Age, breaks = c(0, 30, 50, 65, 100),
                   labels = c("18-30", "31-50", "51-65", "65+")),
    Hypertension_Baseline = ifelse(SysBP_0m >= 140 | DiaBP_0m >= 90, 
                                   "Hypertensive", "Normal"),
    BMI_Category = cut(BMI, breaks = c(0, 18.5, 25, 30, 100),
                       labels = c("Underweight", "Normal", "Overweight", "Obese"))
  )

# Time series
bp_time <- bp_data %>%
  select(PatientID, TreatmentGroup, SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m, SysBP_6m) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("SysBP"),
               names_to = "Time", values_to = "SysBP") %>%
  mutate(Months = as.numeric(gsub("SysBP_|m", "", Time)))

# Summary data
bp_summary <- bp_time %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup, Months) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ci_data <- bp_time %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup, Months) %>%
  summarise(Mean = mean(SysBP), SE = sd(SysBP) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop")

# Custom theme from Module 3
theme_clinical_report <- function(base_size = 12, base_family = "serif") {
  theme_bw(base_size = base_size, base_family = base_family) +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = base_family),
    plot.title = element_text(size = base_size * 1.3, face = "bold", 
                              hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = base_size * 1.1, hjust = 0.5,
                                 color = "gray30", margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9, hjust = 1,
                                face = "italic", color = "gray50"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = base_size * 1.1, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9, color = "gray20"),
    axis.line = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "gray90", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "gray40", fill = NA, linewidth = 1),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(size = base_size, face = "bold"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    legend.key = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
  )
}

What ggplot2 Cannot Do Well
While ggplot2 is powerful, it has limitations:

Mosaic plots / Marimekko charts - Better with ggmosaic or base R mosaicplot()
3D plots - Not natively supported, use plotly or rgl
Network graphs - Use ggraph or igraph
Interactive plots - Limited, need plotly::ggplotly() or ggiraph
Sankey diagrams - Use ggalluvial or networkD3
Circular plots (beyond polar) - Use circlize
Very complex statistical diagrams - May need specialized packages

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4
text:
Common Pitfalls to Avoid

Mapping constants inside aes() - Use fixed values outside aes
Too many aesthetics - Limit to 3-4 visual encodings max
Poor color choices - Always test for colorblind accessibility
Overplotting - Use alpha, jitter, or facets
Misleading axes - Always start at zero for bar charts
Too much clutter - Remove unnecessary grid lines, legends, or decorations
Inconsistent themes - Use theme_set() for consistency
Ignoring aspect ratios - Consider final output dimensions
Not saving properly - Use appropriate format and resolution
Forgetting reproducibility - Set seed, document packages

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4
text:
Best Practices Checklist
Before finalizing visualizations:

Color: Use colorblind-friendly palettes (viridis, ColorBrewer)
Contrast: Ensure sufficient contrast between elements
Text size: Minimum 10pt for body text, 12pt+ for titles
Redundancy: Don’t rely on color alone (use shape, pattern, labels)
Simplicity: Remove unnecessary elements
Labels: Clear, descriptive axis labels and titles
Alt text: Provide text description for screen readers
Print: Test in grayscale/black & white
Simulation: Test with colorblind simulator
Font: Use readable fonts (avoid decorative fonts)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4
text:
The ggplot2 Building Process


Code
ggplot(data, aes(x = var1, y = var2)) +           # 1. Data + Aesthetics
  geom_point(aes(color = var3, size = var4)) +     # 2. Geometry + Local aes
  scale_color_viridis_d() +                        # 3. Scales
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 6)) +         # 4. More scales
  facet_wrap(~ var5) +                             # 5. Facets
  labs(title = "My Plot",                          # 6. Labels
       x = "X Label", y = "Y Label") +
  theme_minimal() +                                # 7. Theme
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",                # 8. Theme customization
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4
text:
Key Takeaways

Grammar of Graphics provides a systematic framework for building visualizations
Layering is fundamental - data → aesthetics → geometries → scales → themes
Aesthetics map data to visual properties (inside aes())
Geoms are the building blocks - choose appropriately for your data type
Themes control appearance - use built-in or create custom ones
Colors matter - always consider colorblind accessibility
Scales control how data maps to aesthetics - customize breaks, limits, labels
Facets enable small multiples for comparing groups
Consistency is key - use global themes and organizational standards
Know ggplot2’s limitations and when to use alternatives

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Setup: Load Data


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readxl)
library(ggthemes)  # For additional themes

# Load and prepare data
bp_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx") %>%
  mutate(
    SysBP_Change = SysBP_6m - SysBP_0m,
    AgeGroup = cut(Age, breaks = c(0, 30, 50, 65, 100),
                   labels = c("18-30", "31-50", "51-65", "65+")),
    Hypertension_Baseline = ifelse(SysBP_0m >= 140 | DiaBP_0m >= 90, 
                                   "Hypertensive", "Normal"),
    BMI_Category = cut(BMI, breaks = c(0, 18.5, 25, 30, 100),
                       labels = c("Underweight", "Normal", "Overweight", "Obese"))
  )

# Time series data
bp_time <- bp_data %>%
  select(PatientID, TreatmentGroup, SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m, SysBP_6m) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("SysBP"),
               names_to = "Time", values_to = "SysBP") %>%
  mutate(Months = as.numeric(gsub("SysBP_|m", "", Time)))

bp_summary <- bp_time %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup, Months) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Global vs Local Aesthetics

Global aesthetics: Defined in ggplot(), apply to all layers
Local aesthetics: Defined in geom_*(), apply to specific layer
Local aesthetics override global aesthetics
Use global for shared mappings, local for layer-specific mappings



Code
ggplot(data, aes(x = var1, y = var2)) +          # Global
  geom_point(aes(color = var3)) +                 # Local (adds color)
  geom_smooth()                                   # Uses global only

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Global Aesthetics Example




Code
# Global color applies to both layers
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m, 
           color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)



Both geom_point() and geom_smooth() use the color mapping

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Local Aesthetics Override




Code
# Local aesthetic overrides global
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = TreatmentGroup), 
             size = 3, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              color = "black", linewidth = 1.5)



Points are colored by treatment, but smooth line is black

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
section: Aesthetic Mapping: Inside vs Outside aes()
text:
Aesthetic Mapping: Inside vs Outside aes()




Code
# MAPPED to data (inside aes)
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,
           color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_point(size = 3)

# FIXED value (outside aes)
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", size = 3)



Key rule: Inside aes() = mapped to data, Outside = fixed value

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Common Pitfall: Mapping Constants




Code
# WRONG - Don't map constants
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,
           color = "blue")) +        # ❌
  geom_point()

# CORRECT - Set fixed values outside aes
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")         # ✓

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
facet_wrap(): Single Variable Faceting




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ TreatmentGroup) +
  theme_minimal()

text:

Code

       aes(x = BMI, y = Cholesterol)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "darkred") +

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
facet_grid(): Two Variable Grid




Code

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Free Scales in Facets




Code
# Create data with different ranges
smoking_bp <- bp_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(SmokingStatus)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(SysBP_0m, DiaBP_0m),
               names_to = "BP_Type",
               values_to = "Value")

ggplot(smoking_bp, aes(x = SmokingStatus, y = Value)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ BP_Type, scales = "free_y")



scales: “fixed” (default), “free”, “free_x”, “free_y”

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Facets with Multiple Geoms




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              color = "darkred", se = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ TreatmentGroup) +
  theme_minimal()



Each facet gets all layers - points and smooth line

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Complex Faceting Example




Code
# Handle missing data
bp_complete <- bp_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(ExerciseFreq))

ggplot(bp_complete, 
       aes(x = AgeGroup, y = SysBP_Change,
           fill = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ ExerciseFreq, ncol = 3) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = 
          element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Theme System Overview

Themes control non-data elements of plots
Affect: fonts, colors, backgrounds, grid lines, axes
ggplot2 includes 8 built-in complete themes
Each theme suited for different contexts
Can be customized further with theme() function


Basic usage: + theme_minimal()

ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Region, y = SysBP_0m,

  geom_boxplot() +

Best for: General exploratory analysis, default choice

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
section: Choosing the Right Visualization for Your Data
text:
Choosing the Right Visualization for Your Data
A Practical Framework Based on Analytical Goals

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
Your Roadmap for Visualization Selection

Identify Your Data Type

What kind of data do you have? (Numeric, Categorical, Temporal, etc.)

Define Your Analytical Goal

What do you want to communicate? (Compare, Distribute, Show Relationships, etc.)

Select the Appropriate Chart

What visualization best achieves your goal?

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
Color-Coded Framework









Goal
Symbol
Question
Purpose




Distribution
●
“What’s the spread?”
Show data spread, shape, outliers


Correlation
●
“How do things relate?”
Show relationships between variables


Ranking
●
“What’s the order?”
Compare values in order


Part of Whole
●
“What’s the composition?”
Show proportions/percentages


Evolution
●
“How does it change over time?”
Track trends and changes


Maps
●
“Where is it located?”
Geographic/spatial distribution


Flow
●
“How does it move?”
Movement, transitions, journeys

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
section: Quick Reference - What Each Color Means
text:
Quick Reference - What Each Color Means

● Gold/Yellow = Distribution - Shows data spread, frequency, shape, outliers
● Blue = Correlation - Shows relationships, associations between variables
● Green = Ranking - Shows order, comparison of values, top/bottom
● Red/Salmon = Part of Whole - Shows composition, proportions, percentages
● Light Blue = Evolution - Shows trends, changes over time, trajectories
● Purple = Maps - Shows geographic/spatial distribution, location-based data
● Pink/Tan = Flow - Shows movement, transitions, journeys, hierarchies

Tip: When you see a colored dot next to a chart name, it tells you what analytical goal that chart serves best!

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
The 6 Data Type Categories








Data Type
Definition
Examples




Numeric
Continuous measurements
Age, weight, blood pressure, lab values


Categoric
Discrete categories/groups
Gender, disease status, treatment type


Ordinal
Ordered categories
Likert scale, tumor stages, severity levels


Time Series
Temporal/chronological data
Monthly incidence, patient vitals over time


Relational
Connections/networks
Patient pathways, disease networks


Map
Geographic/spatial data
Regional disease rates, location coordinates

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
How Variables Combine
SINGLE VARIABLE
├── Numeric → Histogram, Density, Boxplot
├── Categoric → Bar, Pie, Lollipop
├── Ordinal → Ordered Bar, Cumulative Frequency
├── Time Series → Line, Area
├── Map → Choropleth, Bubble Map
└── Relational → Network Graph

BIVARIATE (TWO VARIABLES)
├── Numeric × Numeric → Scatter, Hexbin, Bubble
├── Numeric × Categoric → Boxplot, Violin, Grouped Bar
├── Categoric × Categoric → Grouped/Stacked Bar, Mosaic, Heatmap
├── Time Series × Numeric → Multi-line, Stacked Area
├── Time Series × Categoric → Faceted Line, Interaction Plot
└── Any + Relational → Sankey, Chord

MULTIVARIATE (3+ VARIABLES)
├── Numeric × Numeric × Numeric → Bubble, Faceted Scatter
├── Numeric × Multiple Categoric → Faceted Box/Violin, Interaction
├── Multiple Categoric × Multiple Categoric → Sankey, Sunburst, Treemap
├── Time Series × Multiple Variables → Ridgeline, Faceted Line
└── Hierarchical → Treemap, Sunburst, Hierarchical Edge Bundling

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution | ● Ranking | ● Part of Whole
Chart Options:

Bar Chart ● (counts/frequencies)
Lollipop Chart ● (alternative to bar, especially for long lists)
Cleveland Dot Plot ● (ranked comparison)
Pie Chart ● (≤5 categories only, part-to-whole)
Doughnut Chart ● (like pie, better labels)
Circular Bar Plot ● (aesthetic alternative)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease prevalence by state
Hospitalization by insurance type
Comorbidity frequency distribution

Decision Guide:

Few categories (<5) and need part-of-whole → Pie/Doughnut
Few-moderate categories → Bar chart (horizontal if long names)
Many categories (>8) → Lollipop or Cleveland dot
Need ranking emphasis → Ordered bar or lollipop

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution | ● Part of Whole (Ordered)
Chart Options:

Ordered Bar Chart ● (maintain categorical order)
Ordered Dot Plot ●
Cumulative Frequency Plot ● (especially for Likert scales)
Frequency Polygon ● (smooth trend)

Healthcare Examples:

Patient satisfaction (Likert: 1=Very Unsatisfied to 5=Very Satisfied)
Tumor stages frequency (Stage I → II → III → IV)
Pain severity distribution (None → Mild → Moderate → Severe)
Risk level counts (Low → Medium → High)

Decision Guide:

Likert scales → Stacked ordered bar or cumulative frequency
Natural progression (stages, severity) → Maintain order on axis
Show accumulation → Cumulative frequency plot
Compare between groups → Grouped ordered bar

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution
Chart Options:

Histogram ● (shows bin structure, distribution shape)
Density Plot ● (smooth, continuous estimate)
Boxplot ● (summary: median, quartiles, outliers)
Violin Plot ● (distribution + boxplot combined)
Dot/Strip Plot ● (individual points, best for small n)

Healthcare Examples:

Age distribution in cohort
Blood pressure measurements in population
Lab values (HbA1c, cholesterol, creatinine)
Hospital length of stay

Decision Guide:



Scenario
Best Choice
Why




n < 20
Dot/Strip plot
See every point


n = 20-100
Histogram + Boxplot
Balance detail & summary


n > 100
Density plot
Smooth, reduces noise


Want outliers
Boxplot
Shows extreme values clearly


Want shape details
Violin plot
Shows multimodality, skewness

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution
Chart Options:

Line Chart ● (standard for continuous time data)
Area Chart ● (emphasizes magnitude/volume)
Streamgraph ● (stacked area with flowing theme)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease incidence trends over years
Hospital admission rates monthly
COVID-19 case counts by week
Patient vital signs during hospitalization

Decision Guide:

Single series, continuous time → Line chart
Show cumulative volume → Area chart
Multiple series, show total → Stacked area
Sparse time points → Line chart with markers

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Maps
Chart Options:

Choropleth Map ● (color-coded by region)
Bubble Map ● (circles sized by value)
Heat Map ● (geographic intensity)
Dot Map ● (point locations)

Healthcare Examples:

Regional disease rates (e.g., TB incidence by state in India)
Hospital bed density by district
Maternal mortality ratios by region
Vaccination coverage by area

Decision Guide:

Show rate/percentage by region → Choropleth
Show absolute counts by location → Bubble map
Show intensity/density → Heat map
Specific point locations matter → Dot map

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Correlation | ● Distribution
Chart Options:

Scatter Plot ● (relationship between two continuous variables)
Hexbin Plot ● (2D histogram for dense data)
2D Density Plot ● (contour or heatmap of overlapping points)
Bubble Plot ● (3rd variable via size or color)

Healthcare Examples:

Age vs BMI (body mass relationship)
HbA1c vs Blood Glucose (glycemic control markers)
Creatinine vs eGFR (kidney function)
Systolic vs Diastolic Blood Pressure

Decision Guide:



Scenario
Best Choice




Moderate sample, clear pattern
Scatter plot


Large n, lots of overplotting
Hexbin or 2D density


Want 3rd variable shown
Bubble (size) or color gradient


Focused region interest
Zoomed scatter with annotations

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution | ● Correlation (Comparison)
Chart Options:

Boxplot ● (median, quartiles, outliers by group)
Violin Plot ● (distribution shape by group)
Jittered Dot/Strip/Beeswarm Plot ● (individual points by group)
Bar Chart with Error Bars ● (mean/median ± SD/IQR)
Cleveland Dot Plot ● (ranked group means)

Healthcare Examples:

HbA1c levels across treatment arms
BMI by disease status (healthy vs diabetic vs obese)
Blood pressure by gender
Hospital length of stay by admission type

Decision Guide:



Sample Size
Distribution Focus
Summary Focus




n < 30
Dot/Strip + Boxplot
Not recommended


n = 30-100
Violin or Boxplot
Bar with error bars


n > 100
Violin plot
Density overlay + mean line


Outliers matter
Boxplot + jitter
Always show


Group ranking focus
Ranked dots
Lollipop chart

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Correlation (Probability)
Chart Options:

Logistic Regression Curve ● (smooth probability line)
Density Overlay ● (stacked densities by category)
Grouped Histogram/Density ● (overlapping distributions)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease presence/absence across age ranges
Treatment response (yes/no) by baseline score
Adverse event (yes/no) by medication dose
Mortality (yes/no) by APACHE score

Visualization:

X-axis: Numeric predictor (age, score, dose)
Y-axis: Probability or proportion
Two groups shown as overlapping curves or stacked

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
section: ● Distribution | ● Ranking | ● Part of Whole | ● Correlation
text:
● Distribution | ● Ranking | ● Part of Whole | ● Correlation
Chart Options:

Grouped Bar Chart ● (side-by-side comparison)
Dodged Bar Chart ● (similar to grouped)
Stacked Bar Chart ● (shows totals + composition)
Stacked Bar (Proportional) ● (percentage/100% stacked)
Mosaic Plot ● (area ∝ frequency, shows association)
Heatmap ● (color intensity for cell frequencies)

Healthcare Examples:

Gender vs Disease status (M/F vs HIV+/HIV-)
Treatment arm vs Adverse event (Drug A/B vs AE Yes/No)
Hospital site vs Patient outcome (Site 1-3 vs Recovered/Died)
Risk level by comorbidity count

Decision Guide:



Goal
Best Chart




Compare totals & subgroups
Grouped bar


Show composition per category
Stacked bar


Show percentages only
Stacked bar (proportional)


Detect association strength
Mosaic or heatmap


Many categories, dense
Heatmap with color gradient

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution (Ordered)
Chart Options:

Ordered Boxplot ● (boxplot by ordinal groups, maintaining order)
Ordered Violin Plot ● (violin by ordinal groups)
Ordered Jittered Points ● (points by group, groups ordered)

Healthcare Examples:

Medication efficacy vs dose level (Low/Medium/High)
Lab value vs disease severity (Stage I-IV)
Pain score vs treatment intensity (Mild/Moderate/Severe)
Functional status vs age group (Young/Middle/Elderly)

Key Point:

Always maintain explicit ordering on axis
Example: Severity I → II → III → IV (not random order)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution | ● Correlation (Trend)
Chart Options:

Line Chart ● (single series over time)
Multi-line Chart ● (multiple series overlay)
Area Chart ● (cumulative volume over time)
Stacked Area Chart ● (composition over time)
Connected Scatter ● (if sparse time points)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease incidence trends over years (single disease)
Patient vital signs over hospital stay (temperature, BP, HR)
Medication effectiveness over weeks (Drug A vs B)
Mortality rates over decades by region

Decision Guide:

Single series → Line chart
Few series (2-3) to compare → Multi-line chart
Many series, want to show total → Stacked area
Series showing parts of whole → Stacked area
Sparse measurements → Line with markers or connected scatter

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution (By Group) | ● Correlation (Group Comparison)
Chart Options:

Grouped Line Chart ● (separate lines for each group)
Faceted Line Chart ● (separate subplots per group)
Grouped Area Chart ● (stacked or overlapping)
Interaction Plot ● (lines intersecting showing interaction)
Ribbon Chart ● (flowing bands representing groups)

Healthcare Examples:

Mortality rate trends (gender comparison: M vs F)
Hospital admission trends by institution (5-year follow-up)
Drug effectiveness over time by treatment arm
Complication rates by age group over study period

Decision Guide:

Few groups (2-3) → Multi-line chart
Many groups (5+) → Faceted line plots
Want to show total + groups → Stacked area
Interaction patterns matter → Interaction plot (lines cross)
Space constraints → Faceting better than overlapping

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution (Ordered) | ● Part of Whole (Ordered)
Chart Options:

Ordered Grouped Bar Chart ● (bars by category, groups ordered)
Ordered Stacked Bar ● (stacked, ordinal categories in order)
Faceted Ordered Bar ● (subplots maintaining order)

Healthcare Examples:

Patient satisfaction (Likert: 1-5) by hospital ward
Pain severity (None/Mild/Moderate/Severe) by treatment type
Risk level (Low/Med/High) by comorbidity count
Functional status by treatment arm

Key Point:

Maintain ordinal ordering on one axis
Example: Satisfaction scale always: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
3+ Continuous Variables | ● Correlation
Chart Options:

Bubble Plot ● (x, y, size = 3rd; color/opacity = 4th)
Faceted Scatter ● (scatter by groups, multiple subplots)
3D Scatter (NOT recommended: distorts perception)

Healthcare Examples:

Age vs BMI (size=cholesterol, color=treatment arm)
HbA1c vs glucose (size=insulin, faceted by gender)
Systolic vs diastolic BP (colored by smoking status)

Decision Guide:

3 variables → Bubble plot (x, y, size)
4 variables → Bubble + color
5+ variables → Multiple faceted plots (don’t try to cram)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Correlation Matrix
Chart Options:

Correlation Matrix ● (numeric table of coefficients)
Correlogram ● (heatmap with color intensity = correlation strength)
Scatter Plot Matrix ● (pairwise scatter plots)

Healthcare Examples:

Lab inter-correlations: glucose, insulin, triglycerides, HDL, LDL
Vital signs correlations: BP, HR, RR, O2 saturation, temperature
Biomarker relationships in cohort study

Visualization:

Color intensity (warm = positive, cool = negative)
Cell size may represent correlation strength
Diagonal typically = 1.0 (variable with itself)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution (Faceted) | ● Correlation (Interaction)
Chart Options:

Faceted Boxplot/Violin ● (boxplot per group, subplots for 3rd variable)
Interaction Plot ● (lines connecting means by two factors)
Faceted Scatter + regression lines ● (by groups)

Healthcare Examples:

HbA1c by treatment type, faceted by gender (4 subplots: 2 treat × 2 gender)
Lab values by disease status, colored by age group
Drug efficacy by dose level, faceted by patient comorbidity

Visualization Strategy:

Primary grouping on axis
Secondary grouping via facets or colors
Show interactions: do lines cross? Do patterns differ?

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution (Advanced) | ● Distribution (Temporal)
Chart Options:

Multi-line Chart with Faceting ● (separate subplots per group)
Ridgeline Plot ● (distribution by group, stacked vertically)
Slope Chart ● (start → end values, multiple series)
Animated Time Series ● (interactive exploration)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease incidence over years, separate lines by region (5 regions)
Patient vitals during admission, faceted by treatment arm
Hospital census by time, colored by department

Decision Guide:

Multiple time series + groups → Faceted multi-line
Distribution evolution over time → Ridgeline plot
Show change from start to end → Slope chart

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Flow | ● Part of Whole (Hierarchical)
Chart Options:

Sankey Diagram ● (flow from one category to another)
Alluvial Diagram ● (similar to Sankey, broader flows)
Treemap ● (nested rectangles for hierarchy)
Sunburst Chart ● (nested circles/rings for hierarchy)

Healthcare Examples:

Sankey: Patient flow (admission → diagnostic → treatment → discharge)
Alluvial: Disease progression stages (diagnosis → worsening/improvement → outcome)
Treemap: Hospital structure (Region → Hospital → Department → Ward)
Sunburst: Disease classification (Category → Subcategory → Specific condition)

Decision Guide:

Flow/transition/journey → Sankey or Alluvial
Nested hierarchy/parts → Treemap or Sunburst

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Flow | ● Correlation (Connections)
Chart Options:

Sankey Diagram ● (directional flows between nodes)
Chord Diagram ● (bi-directional relationships, circular)
Network Graph ● (nodes + edges, force-directed layout)
Arc Diagram ● (nodes in line, arcs show connections)

Healthcare Examples:

Sankey: Patient journeys through clinic system
Chord: Disease co-occurrence patterns (patient network)
Network: Hospital referral patterns (which hospitals refer to which)
Arc: Comorbidity networks (which diseases co-occur)

Visualization:

Nodes = entities (patients, diseases, hospitals)
Edges/arcs/flows = relationships (referral, co-occurrence)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Part of Whole | ● Flow
Chart Options:

Treemap ● (nested rectangles, size ∝ value)
Sunburst Chart ● (nested circles, size ∝ value)
Hierarchical Edge Bundling ● (connections in hierarchy)

Healthcare Examples:

Treemap: Hospital admissions by Region → State → Hospital → Department (size = admission count)
Sunburst: Disease classification by Category → Subcategory → Specific condition → ICD code
Hierarchical Edge Bundling: Referral patterns between hospitals at different levels

Decision Guide:

Static hierarchy focus → Treemap
Want circular aesthetic → Sunburst
Complex relationships in hierarchy → Hierarchical edge bundling

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Flow | ● Part of Whole
Waterfall Chart

Shows cumulative effect of sequential positive/negative values
Healthcare Example: Patient survival from enrollment → screening loss → randomization → completion

Start: 1000 enrolled
Drop: -50 screening failures
Drop: -30 withdrawn consent
End: 920 completed


Funnel Chart

Stages in a process, showing attrition at each step
Healthcare Example: Hospital admission pipeline

Emergency triage: 500
Admitted: 400 (20% filtered out)
Discharged: 350 (12.5% transferred)
Readmitted: 30 (8.6% recurrent)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution (Advanced) | ● Distribution (Temporal)
Streamgraph

Stacked area with flowing, organic theme
Example: Emergency admissions over time, stacked by department

Total volume trends visible + department composition


Calendar Heatmap

Daily/weekly patterns across entire year
Example: Hospital occupancy by day of week

Darker = higher occupancy
Pattern reveals peak days/seasons


Frequency Polygon

Line connecting histogram bins
Example: Age distribution comparison between cohorts

Multiple overlaid frequency polygons

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution (Text) | ● Correlation (Networks)
Word Cloud

Text frequency visualization, size = occurrence
Limitation: More visual impact than analytic precision
Healthcare Use: Patient feedback themes, common symptoms

Arc Diagram

Network relationships with improved readability over hairball graphs
Example: Disease comorbidity network, cleaner than typical network graph

Hierarchical Edge Bundling

Complex relationship networks with hierarchy
Example: Referral patterns between hospitals (different organizational levels)

text:
Scenario: “Quarterly revenue by product category over 2 years”
Step 1: Identify Data Type

Time component: Quarterly (Time Series)
Product component: Multiple categories (Categoric)
Revenue component: Continuous (Numeric)
Combined: Time Series + Categoric + Numeric

Step 2: Define Analytical Goal

Primary: ● Evolution (how revenue changes over time)
Secondary: ● Correlation (how categories compare)

Step 3: Chart Options









Option
Chart Type
Pros
Cons




A
Multi-line chart ●
Clear trend per product
Can be cluttered if >5 products


B
Stacked area ●
Show total + composition
Hard to compare individual products


C
Faceted line charts ●
Each product clear
Uses more space


D
Grouped bar chart ●

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
section: Scenario: “HbA1c levels across three treatment arms over 12 months”
text:
Scenario: “HbA1c levels across three treatment arms over 12 months”
Step 1: Identify Data Type

Time component: Baseline, 6mo, 12mo (Time Series - discrete)
Group component: 3 treatment arms (Categoric)
Outcome component: HbA1c values (Numeric)
Combined: Time Series + Categoric + Numeric

Step 2: Define Analytical Goal

Primary: ● Evolution (trajectories over follow-up)
Secondary: ● Correlation (do arms differ?)
Tertiary: ● Distribution (spread within each arm at each timepoint)

Step 3: Chart Options








Option
Chart Type
Visualization




A
Multi-line ± CI ●
One line per arm, shaded confidence bands


B
Faceted violin plots ●
3 subplots (one per arm), violin at each timepoint


C
Spaghetti plot ●
Individual patient trajectories, color-coded by arm


D
Interaction plot ●
Means connected by lines, x-axis = timepoint

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
section: Scenario: “Top 10 competitors’ market share over 5 years by region”
text:
Scenario: “Top 10 competitors’ market share over 5 years by region”
Step 1: Identify Data Type

Time: Years (Time Series)
Competitors: 10 categories (Categoric)
Regions: Multiple regions (Categoric)
Market share: Percentage (Numeric)
Dimensions: 4 (too many for single plot!)

Step 2: Define Analytical Goal

● Evolution (trends over time)
● Ranking (who’s leading?)
● Correlation (how do regions differ?)
● Composition (what % of total?)

Step 3: Chart Options







Option
Approach




A
Stacked area per region (faceted: 3-5 subplots) ● ●


B
Grouped multi-line (each region = different color) ●


C
Animated bar chart (top 10 race by region) ● ●


D
Interactive dashboard (toggle region) ●



Decision:

Best static option: Faceted stacked area (shows time, composition, region comparison)
Best interactive: Animated bar or dashboard

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
❌ What NOT to Do
❌ Pie charts with 10+ categories

Why? Human perception fails with small angles
Solution: Use bar chart ●, lollipop ●, or split into multiple pies

❌ 3D charts

Why? Perspective distorts data perception (3D cone/pyramid/sphere)
Solution: Stick to 2D representations

❌ Dual-axis charts

Why? Can mislead by manipulating axis scales
Solution: Use faceting or separate plots instead

❌ Wrong color coding

Why? Color should reinforce analytical goal (not random aesthetic)
Solution: Sequential colors for magnitude, categorical colors for groups

❌ Overplotting (overlapping points)

Why? Can’t see density or exact position
Solution: Use transparency (alpha), jitter, hexbin ●, or density plots ●

❌ Stacked bars for detailed comparison

Why? Only first and last categories are easy to compare
Solution: Use grouped bar ● or faceting for detailed comparison

❌ Too many dimensions on one plot

Why? Cognitive overload, hard to extract insight
Solution: Split into multiple focused visualizations

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
Core Principles for Effective Visualization
✅ Always start with your analytical goal - What question are you answering? (distribute, compare, rank, relate, etc.)
✅ Data types narrow your options significantly - Numeric vs Categoric vs Ordinal vs Temporal vs Spatial
✅ Multiple valid charts may exist—choose based on audience & context - Scientist ≠ Executive ≠ Patient communication
✅ Use color strategically to support your analytical goal - Sequential for magnitude, categorical for groups, diverging for contrasts
✅ Simplicity trumps complexity; avoid unnecessary dimensions - If 3D doesn’t add insight, keep it 2D - If faceting helps clarity, use it
✅ When in doubt, check data-to-viz.com or reference examples - Don’t reinvent the wheel; learn from established best practices
✅ Practice makes perfect—iterate on visualizations - First draft rarely optimal; refine based on feedback

title: Best Practices
text:
Introduction to Data Visualization

“The simple graph has brought more information to the data analyst’s mind than any other device.” - John Tukey


Data visualization transforms complex data into visual insights
Good visualizations tell a story
Poor visualizations mislead or confuse
Every choice matters - especially in healthcare

title: Best Practices
text:
The Big Idea
Can you summarize your message in one sentence?

Your “Big Idea” should be:

Articulate your point of view: What do you want your audience to know?
Convey what’s at stake: Why does this matter?
Be a complete sentence: Not just a topic, but a statement

Example: “We should implement early discharge planning because it reduces readmissions by 35%”

title: Best Practices
section: Principle 1: Choose the Right Chart Type
text:
Principle 1: Choose the Right Chart Type
Match your visualization to your data and message
Different types of data require different visualizations:

Simple text: 1-2 key numbers
Tables: Multiple precise values
Categorical: Bar charts (horizontal preferred)
Continuous over time: Line charts, area charts
Distributions: Histograms, boxplots, violin plots, density plots
Relationships: Scatter plots, correlations
Comparisons: Slopegraphs, small multiples
Part-to-whole: Stacked bars (avoid pie charts)

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Simple Text


Effective: When you have just 1-2 key numbers, text is more impactful than a chart. Makes the metric impossible to miss and allows for immediate comprehension.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Table


Effective: Tables excel when precise values matter and units differ. Better than charts when readers need exact numbers for comparison or reference.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Heatmap


Effective: Heatmaps encode values with color, making patterns instantly visible in large tables. Ideal for spotting trends across two categorical dimensions.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Horizontal Bar Chart


Effective: Horizontal bars are preferred for categorical comparisons. Long labels read naturally, and length comparisons are easier than height comparisons.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Grouped Bar Chart


Effective: Grouped bars allow direct comparison across two categorical variables. The gap between groups creates visual separation that aids comprehension.

title: Best Practices
section: Avoid: Vertical Bars with Long Labels
text:
Avoid: Vertical Bars with Long Labels


Ineffective: Vertical bars with long labels force text rotation, making reading difficult. Horizontal bars solve this problem naturally.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Line Chart


Effective: Line charts emphasize continuity and trend direction over time. The connecting line helps viewers see patterns and predict future values.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Area Chart


Effective: Stacked area charts show both individual trends and cumulative total. The filled areas emphasize volume and make the overall trend prominent.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Multiple Line Series


Effective: Multiple series work when normalized to comparable scales. Different colors distinguish series while the shared timeline enables pattern comparison across variables.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Scatter Plot


Effective: Scatter plots reveal relationships between continuous variables. The trend line and confidence interval quantify the strength and uncertainty of the relationship.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Scatter with Categories


Effective: Adding categories to scatter plots reveals whether relationships hold across subgroups. Parallel slopes suggest consistent effects; diverging slopes indicate interactions.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Boxplot


Effective: Boxplots show distribution shape through quartiles. The box contains 50% of data, whiskers show range, and outliers appear as points - all in one compact visual.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Violin Plot


Effective: Violin plots reveal distribution details that boxplots hide. The width at each point shows density, making bimodal distributions and skewness immediately apparent.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Density Plot


Effective: Density plots show smooth distribution curves, ideal for comparing shapes between groups. Overlapping areas make differences in location, spread, and skewness clear.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Ridgeline Plot


Effective: Ridgeline plots stack density curves for easy comparison across many categories. The slight overlap creates visual flow while maintaining distinct distributions.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Slopegraph


Effective: Slopegraphs excel at showing change between two time points. The slope angle immediately conveys magnitude and direction of change for each entity.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Stacked Bar Chart


Effective: Stacked bars show part-to-whole relationships over time. Total height shows cumulative volume while segment heights reveal individual contributions.

title: Best Practices
section: Avoid: Y-Axis Not Starting at Zero
text:
Avoid: Y-Axis Not Starting at Zero


Ineffective: Truncating the Y-axis on bar charts distorts proportional relationships. What is actually a 3% difference appears as a 3-fold difference due to the missing baseline.

title: Best Practices
text:
Better: Y-Axis Starting at Zero


Effective: Starting bar charts at zero shows true proportions. Now it’s clear that all hospitals perform similarly at high levels with minimal variation.

title: Best Practices
text:
Avoid: Pie Charts


Ineffective: Humans struggle with angle and area estimation. Quick: is Respiratory or Other larger? Pie charts make simple comparisons unnecessarily difficult.

title: Best Practices
text:
Better: Horizontal Bar Chart


Effective: Horizontal bars make comparisons effortless. Rankings are immediately clear, and length differences are precisely perceivable unlike angles in pie charts.

title: Best Practices
text:
Principle 2: Eliminate Clutter
Remove anything that doesn’t add value

Remove chart borders and backgrounds
Lighten or remove gridlines

Remove redundant data labels
Direct labeling > legends (Gestalt principle of connection)
Clean up axis labels
Maximize data-to-ink ratio (Tufte’s principle)

title: Best Practices
text:
Data-to-Ink Ratio: Maximizing Information
Every drop of ink should represent data

Data ink: Ink that represents actual data points
Non-data ink: Gridlines, borders, backgrounds, decorations
Goal: Maximize the ratio of data ink to total ink
Remove chart junk: 3D effects, unnecessary colors, decorative elements
Keep only what serves comprehension

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Default Plot (Cluttered)


Ineffective: Gray background, heavy gridlines, legend requiring eye travel, and borders all compete for attention. The data-to-ink ratio is low - most ink conveys no data.

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Decluttered with Direct Labels


Effective: High data-to-ink ratio achieved by removing backgrounds, excess gridlines, and legend. Direct labels connect to data via proximity (Gestalt principle).

title: Best Practices
text:
Principle 3: Use Preattentive Attributes
Attention with attributes processed in <250ms

Color: Most powerful
Size: Indicates importance
Position: Spatial relationships
Intensity: Bold vs light
Use strategically - don’t dilute attention

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: All Equal (No Focus)


Ineffective: All bars are equal - where should the viewer look? No visual hierarchy means no clear message.

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Strategic Highlighting


Effective: Red instantly draws the eye to the problem. Gray provides context without competing for attention.

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Using Size for Emphasis


Effective: Size combined with color creates a clear hierarchy. The large red point in August demands attention while smaller gray points provide context.

title: Best Practices
text:
Principle 4: Gray and Bold Technique
Use color to highlight, gray to push back

Bold color for what matters most
Gray for supporting context
Maximum one bold color per chart
Creates instant visual hierarchy
Reduces cognitive load

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Too Many Colors


Ineffective: Multiple bold colors fragment attention. When everything demands attention, nothing gets it.

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Gray and Bold Applied


Effective: One bold color directs attention immediately to the problem area. Gray bars provide necessary context without distraction.

title: Best Practices
text:
Principle 5: Think Like a Designer
Visual design principles enhance communication

Accessibility: Colorblind-safe palettes
Alignment: Create invisible structure
White space: Let your data breathe
Contrast: Guide the eye
Typography: Readable, professional fonts

title: Best Practices
text:
Accessibility: Colorblind-Safe Palettes


Always use colorblind-safe palettes. Approximately 8% of men and 0.5% of women have color vision deficiency. Blue-orange combinations work for nearly everyone.

title: Best Practices
text:
Design Principles: Alignment & Spacing


Effective design: Generous margins, aligned text, strategic white space, and clear visual hierarchy make the message instantly clear and professional.

title: Best Practices
text:
Using Annotations Strategically


Annotations tell the story. The chart clearly shows what happened, when it happened, and why it matters - the viewer doesn’t need to guess.

title: Best Practices
text:
Before/After: Design Transformation


Design transformation: horizontal orientation, strategic color, descriptive title, reference line, and clean styling create a professional, focused message.

title: Best Practices
section: Principle 6: Tell a Story with Data
text:
Principle 6: Tell a Story with Data
Transform insights into narrative

Beginning: Set context (current state)
Middle: Show the problem/opportunity
End: Recommend action
Use descriptive titles that state your point
Guide your audience through the data

title: Best Practices
text:
Narrative vs Descriptive Titles


Narrative titles tell the story. The right chart doesn’t just show data - it communicates the achievement and its magnitude immediately.

title: Best Practices
text:
Small Multiples: Powerful Comparisons


Small multiples enable comparison. Same scales across panels make differences immediately visible. Trend lines show improvement rates at a glance.

title: Best Practices
text:
Small Multiples: Distribution Comparisons


Distribution comparison made easy. Procedure C clearly clusters below the target with minimal variation, while Procedure D shows high variability and longer recovery.

title: Best Practices
text:
Complete Story Example


Complete narrative: Beginning (context with peers), middle (intervention and dramatic improvement), end (current state showing success). Every element supports the story.

title: Best Practices
text:
Advanced Topic: Handling Uncertainty


Show uncertainty honestly. Confidence intervals demonstrate that even accounting for variability, the new treatment shows meaningful improvement over the standard.

title: Best Practices
text:
Advanced Topic: Distribution of Uncertainty


Full distribution view. The minimal overlap between distributions shows that the new treatment improvement is robust, not just a result of a few outliers.

title: Best Practices
text:
Advanced Topic: Correlation Matrices


Multivariate relationships at a glance. Correlation matrices reveal complex patterns - here showing BMI and stress as strongest blood pressure predictors.

title: Best Practices
text:
Common Pitfall: Cherry-Picking Time Ranges


Always show full context. The “growth” story disappears when viewing the complete timeline. Cherry-picking ranges is a common way to mislead.

title: Best Practices
section: Edge Case: When Breaking Rules Makes Sense
text:
Edge Case: When Breaking Rules Makes Sense


Breaking the “zero baseline” rule is appropriate when zero is meaningless (temperature, stock prices, pH). The focus should be on clinically meaningful variation.

title: Best Practices
text:
Summary: Six Core Principles

Choose the Right Chart Type - Match visualization to data and message
Eliminate Clutter - Maximize data-to-ink ratio
Use Preattentive Attributes - Guide attention strategically
Apply Gray and Bold - Create visual hierarchy
Think Like a Designer - Professional, accessible presentation
Tell a Story - Transform insights into narrative

title: Best Practices
text:
Key Takeaways

Every choice matters - color, position, size, titles
Less is more - remove everything that doesn’t serve the message
Context is crucial - never cherry-pick data ranges
Accessibility counts - use colorblind-safe palettes
Focus attention - one bold color, clear hierarchy
Tell the story - guide your audience to action

title: Best Practices
text:
When to Break the Rules
Rules are guidelines, not laws

Zero baseline: not for temperature, stock prices, or indices
Pie charts: acceptable for simple two-part comparisons
Multiple colors: when showing categorical data without hierarchy
The test: Does breaking the rule serve your audience better?
Always ask: Am I making the data clearer or just different?

title: Best Practices
text:
Resources & Further Learning


Books

Storytelling with Data - Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic
The Visual Display of Quantitative Information - Edward Tufte
Good Charts - Scott Berinato


Online

ggplot2 documentation
R Graph Gallery
Data Visualization Society
Storytelling with Data blog

title: Best Practices
text:
Thank You!
Questions?

Remember: The goal of data visualization is not to make beautiful charts - it’s to communicate insights that drive better decisions.
“The greatest value of a picture is when it forces us to notice what we never expected to see.” - John Tukey

title: Iteration: Doing the Same Thing Many Times
text:
Medical analyses repeat: the same summary for 12 variables, the same test for 5 outcomes, the same plot for each district. Copy-pasting code 12 times is how mistakes get in (one copy keeps an old variable name). This page shows four safer ways, from simplest to most general. Data: the NCD survey (data/ncd_survey.csv).

library(tidyverse)
ncd <- read_csv(c("../data/ncd_survey.csv", "data/ncd_survey.csv")[file.exists(c("../data/ncd_survey.csv", "data/ncd_survey.csv"))][1], show_col_types = FALSE)




ncd |> summarise(across(c(sbp, dbp, bmi), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
    sbp   dbp   bmi
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1  132.  59.7  23.0



across(columns, function) applies the function to each column inside summarise() or mutate().
\(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) is a small unnamed function; x stands for “the column”.
Pick columns by name, c(a, b), or by type, where(is.numeric).
Several functions at once, with names:


ncd |> summarise(across(c(sbp, bmi), list(mean = \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), sd = \(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))))

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  sbp_mean sbp_sd bmi_mean bmi_sd
     <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>
1     132.   16.8     23.0   3.58



ncd |> mutate(across(c(sbp, dbp), \(x) x / 10)) |> select(sbp, dbp) |> head(3)    # the same change to two columns

# A tibble: 3 × 2
    sbp   dbp
  <dbl> <dbl>
1  13.1   5.7
2  13.5   6.1
3  12.7   5.7






for (v in c("sbp", "dbp", "bmi")) {
  cat(v, ": mean", round(mean(ncd[[v]], na.rm = TRUE), 1), "\n")
}

sbp : mean 132.3 
dbp : mean 59.7 
bmi : mean 23 



for (v in <items>) { <what to do> } runs the block once for each item, and v holds the current item.
ncd[[v]] picks the column whose name is stored in v (ncd$v would look for a column called “v”).
A loop prints or stores results; it only shows output if you ask (print(), cat()).
A loop that adds up:


total <- 0
for (i in 1:4) total <- total + i
total

[1] 10






sapply(ncd[c("sbp", "dbp", "bmi")], mean, na.rm = TRUE)       # a named vector of means

      sbp       dbp       bmi 
132.28500  59.68833  22.95258 



# one t-test per outcome, results kept in a tidy table
outcomes <- c("sbp", "dbp", "bmi")
map_dfr(outcomes, \(y) {
  t <- t.test(reformulate("sex", y), data = ncd)
  tibble(outcome = y, difference = unname(diff(rev(t$estimate))), p = t$p.value)
})

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  outcome difference       p
  <chr>        <dbl>   <dbl>
1 sbp         -3.78  0.00595
2 dbp         -1.61  0.0385 
3 bmi          0.387 0.193  



map() / sapply() return one result per item, collected for you: no empty vector to grow by hand.
reformulate("sex", y) builds the formula y ~ sex from text, so the loop can change the outcome.
map_dfr() stacks tibbles into one table; map_dbl() returns numbers.





pct_above <- function(x, cut) {
  mean(x >= cut, na.rm = TRUE) * 100      # the last value is returned
}
pct_above(ncd$sbp, 140)

[1] 32

pct_above(ncd$bmi, 30)

[1] 2.405498



A function has arguments (x, cut), a body in { }, and returns its last expression.
Write one when you copy the same 3 or more lines twice. Name it for what it does.
Test it on a case where you know the answer: pct_above(c(1, 5, 10, 20), 10) should be 50.










Warning




Growing a vector inside a loop (res <- c(res, new)) is slow and error-prone; use sapply() / map().
Forgetting na.rm = TRUE inside the function you repeat: one NA turns every result into NA.
ncd$v vs ncd[[v]]: with the variable name in v, use [[ ]].
Overwriting the original data in a loop; save results to a new object.
Many tests at once means many p-values: see multiple testing on the Statistical Tests page.

pct_above(ncd$bmi, 30)

[1] 2.405498



A function has arguments (x, cut), a body in { }, and returns its last expression.
Write one when you copy the same 3 or more lines twice. Name it for what it does.
Test it on a case where you know the answer: pct_above(c(1, 5, 10, 20), 10) should be 50.

title: Iteration: Doing the Same Thing Many Times
text:
Warning




Growing a vector inside a loop (res <- c(res, new)) is slow and error-prone; use sapply() / map().
Forgetting na.rm = TRUE inside the function you repeat: one NA turns every result into NA.
ncd$v vs ncd[[v]]: with the variable name in v, use [[ ]].
Overwriting the original data in a loop; save results to a new object.
Many tests at once means many p-values: see multiple testing on the Statistical Tests page.

Question: Classify baseline BP using clinical guidelines

bp_with_category <- bp_clean |> 
  mutate(
    bp_category = case_when(
      sys_bp_0m < 120 & dia_bp_0m < 80 ~ "Normal",
      sys_bp_0m >= 120 & sys_bp_0m < 130 & dia_bp_0m < 80 ~ "Elevated",
      (sys_bp_0m >= 130 & sys_bp_0m < 140) | 
        (dia_bp_0m >= 80 & dia_bp_0m < 90) ~ "Stage 1",
      sys_bp_0m >= 140 | dia_bp_0m >= 90 ~ "Stage 2"

if_else()

Binary outcomes
Single condition
Simpler syntax

case_when()

Multiple outcomes
Multiple conditions

  condition2 ~ value2,

title: Data Wrangling in R

Why lubridate?

Dates are complex (leap years, time zones, daylight savings)
lubridate makes date operations intuitive
Part of tidyverse but must be loaded separately
Essential for healthcare data with visit dates, follow-ups

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
Age Calculation from Dates

Question: Calculate age from birthdate




Show the code
# Example with made-up birthdates
example_data <- tibble(
  patient_id = 1:3,
  birthdate = ymd(c("1980-05-15", "1965-12-20", "1990-03-08")),
  visit_date = ymd(c("2024-01-15", "2024-01-15", "2024-01-15"))
)

example_data |> 
  mutate(
    age_years = interval(birthdate, visit_date) / years(1),
    age_months = interval(birthdate, visit_date) / months(1)
  )

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
Useful lubridate Functions

Parsing: ymd(), mdy(), dmy() - parse dates
Components: year(), month(), day(), hour(), minute()
Weekdays: wday(), week()
Math: days(), weeks(), months(), years()
Intervals: interval(), time_length()
Current: today(), now()

Error: Object Not Found


Error

bp_data |> 
  select(Patient_ID)


#> Error in `select()`:
#> ! Can't select columns that don't exist.
#> ✖ Column `Patient_ID` doesn't exist.

  select(PatientID)

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
Error: Comparison Operators


Error


Show the code
bp_clean |> 
  filter(age = 50)


#> Error in `filter()`:
#> ! We detected a named input.
#> ℹ This usually means that you've used `=` instead of `==`.
#> ℹ Did you mean `age == 50`?



Solution


Show the code
# Use == for comparison
bp_clean |> 
  filter(age == 50)

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
Error: Pipe Operator


Error


Show the code
bp_clean |> 
  select(age, gender)

#>      age gender
#>    <dbl> <chr> 
#>  1    36 Female
#>  2    79 Male

Show the code
  filter(age > 50)

bp_clean |> 
  select(age, gender) |>

title: Data Wrangling in R
Data Wrangling in R
text:
Tips for Troubleshooting

Build step by step - Add one operation at a time
Check intermediate results - Print after each step
Use View() - Inspect data in RStudio: View(bp_clean)
Read error messages - They usually tell you what’s wrong
Check data types - Use glimpse() or str()
Search for help - Stack Overflow, R documentation

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
Best Practices Summary

Use consistent naming conventions (snake_case)
Clean names early with janitor::clean_names()
Pipe operations for readable code
Check your data at each step
Document your code with comments
Save intermediate results when needed
Test with small samples first

title: Cleaning Messy Data
text:
Real data arrive with inconsistent labels, text in number columns, duplicates and impossible values. Cleaning is not glamorous, but every later result depends on it. This page gives a checklist you can reuse, on a deliberately messy file: data/ncd_messy.csv (313 rows from a field survey).

library(tidyverse); library(janitor)
raw <- read_csv(c("../data/ncd_messy.csv", "data/ncd_messy.csv")[file.exists(c("../data/ncd_messy.csv", "data/ncd_messy.csv"))][1], show_col_types = FALSE)




Never edit the raw file. Write a script that reads it and produces a clean copy; the script is your audit trail.
Inspect before you change anything: glimpse(), summary(), count() of every categorical column, range() of every number.
Change one problem at a time and re-check after each change.
Write down what you changed and how many rows it affected.


glimpse(raw)

Rows: 313
Columns: 9
$ `Pt ID`      <dbl> 249, 288, 67, 226, 201, 132, 10, 244, 176, 1, 47, 291, 11…
$ `Age (yrs)`  <chr> "55", "48", "45", "41", "49", "45", "61", "37", "45", "42…
$ SEX          <chr> "Female", "Male", "male", "Male", "Female", "Male", "Fema…
$ Residence    <chr> "Rural", "Urban", "Rural", "Urban", "Rural", "Rural", "Ru…
$ BMI          <dbl> 24.0, 24.3, 22.1, 21.5, 25.2, 27.5, 28.3, 21.9, 23.0, 26.…
$ `Salt g/day` <chr> "11.7 g", "7.7", "8.5", "9.7", "8.4", "4.1", "10.8", "6.6…
$ SBP          <dbl> 129, 141, 125, 126, 127, 142, 147, 110, 128, 131, 134, 15…
$ Tobacco      <chr> "No", "No", "Yes", "No", "No", "No", "No", "Yes", "No", "…
$ `Visit date` <chr> "2025-01-19", "18/02/2025", "08/01/2025", "06/06/2025", "…


What the glimpse already shows: awkward names (Pt ID, Age (yrs)), Age (yrs) and Salt g/day are text (some values are not plain numbers), and 313 rows although 300 people were surveyed.




d <- raw |> clean_names()
names(d)

[1] "pt_id"      "age_yrs"    "sex"        "residence"  "bmi"       
[6] "salt_g_day" "sbp"        "tobacco"    "visit_date"


clean_names() gives lower-case names with underscores and no spaces or brackets.




count(d, sex)

# A tibble: 8 × 2
  sex        n
  <chr>  <int>
1 F         18
2 FEMALE    13
3 Female    91
4 M         22
5 MALE      13
6 Male      87
7 female    29
8 male      40


Eight spellings for two categories. Standardise, then check again:

d <- d |> mutate(sex = case_when(str_to_lower(sex) %in% c("m", "male") ~ "Male",
                                 str_to_lower(sex) %in% c("f", "female") ~ "Female"))
count(d, sex)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  sex        n
  <chr>  <int>
1 Female   151
2 Male     162

d <- d |> mutate(residence = str_trim(residence))     # "Urban " and "Urban" are different to R
count(d, residence)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  residence     n
  <chr>     <int>
1 Rural       226
2 Urban        87


case_when() returns NA for a label it does not recognise, so a surprise shows up as NA in the check. Do not hide it with a catch-all TRUE ~ ....




d |> filter(is.na(parse_number(age_yrs))) |> count(age_yrs)         # which entries are not numbers?

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  age_yrs     n
  <chr>   <int>
1 unknown     3

d <- d |> mutate(age = parse_number(age_yrs), salt_g = parse_number(salt_g_day))


as.numeric("7.2 g") gives NA; parse_number("7.2 g") reads the number and drops the unit.
Look at what turned into NA, as above, before accepting the conversion.
Dates: visit_date mixes 2025-03-14 and 14/03/2025. Parse each format separately (ymd(), dmy()) and combine, never guess.


d <- d |> mutate(visit = coalesce(ymd(visit_date, quiet = TRUE), dmy(visit_date, quiet = TRUE)))
sum(is.na(d$visit))

[1] 0






summary(d$age)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
  30.00   41.00   49.00   60.43   56.00  999.00       3 

summary(d$sbp)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
    0.0   122.0   132.0   142.7   143.0  1350.0 

d |> filter(age > 120 | sbp < 60 | sbp > 300) |> select(pt_id, age, sbp)

# A tibble: 10 × 3
   pt_id   age   sbp
   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
 1   150    48  1350
 2    99    30     0
 3    20    55  1290
 4    33   999   121
 5    69    55     0
 6    99    30     0
 7   248    49  1100
 8    31   999   143
 9     5   999   138
10   228   999   136



999 is a placeholder for “unknown” (check the codebook); 0 and 1350 for SBP are impossible (the second is probably 135.0 typed with a slip).
Set them to NA; do not delete the rows and do not fill in the mean:


d <- d |> mutate(age = na_if(age, 999), sbp = if_else(sbp < 60 | sbp > 300, NA_real_, sbp))
colSums(is.na(d[c("age", "sbp")]))

age sbp 
  7   6 






nrow(d)

[1] 313

nrow(distinct(d))         # exact copies of a whole row

[1] 303

d |> get_dupes(pt_id) |> select(pt_id, age, sbp, visit_date) |> head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 4
  pt_id   age   sbp visit_date
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>     
1    28    53   155 2025-01-01
2    28    53   155 2025-01-01
3    92    32   121 13/07/2025
4    92    32   121 13/07/2025
5    99    30    NA 2025-07-06
6    99    30    NA 2025-07-06
7   107    58   157 03/01/2025
8   107    58   157 03/01/2025



Exact duplicates (every column the same) are safe to remove with distinct().
The same ID with different values is not an exact duplicate: it may be a repeat visit, a re-entry or a wrong ID. Do not drop one blindly: check the source forms.





tibble(step = c("rows in raw file", "after removing exact duplicates", "age placeholders set to NA", "impossible SBP set to NA"),
       n = c(nrow(raw), nrow(distinct(raw)), sum(raw$`Age (yrs)` == "999", na.rm = TRUE), sum(d$sbp < 60 | d$sbp > 300, na.rm = TRUE)))

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  step                                n
  <chr>                           <int>
1 rows in raw file                  313
2 after removing exact duplicates   303
3 age placeholders set to NA          4
4 impossible SBP set to NA            0


Report this in the methods: it lets a reader see what was done, and lets you repeat it when a corrected file arrives.











Step
Look at
Fix with




Names
names()
clean_names()


Labels
count(col)
case_when(), fct_recode(), str_trim(), str_to_lower()


Types
glimpse(), what becomes NA
parse_number(), ymd() / dmy()


Placeholders, impossible values
summary(), range()
na_if(), if_else(), then report


Duplicates
distinct(), get_dupes()
remove exact copies; investigate repeated IDs


Record
counts before and after
a log in the script

title: Introduction to R
text:
R - Language

Developed in the early 1990s
-Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman at the University of Auckland, New Zealand

A powerful language for statistical computing and graphics

Widely used by statisticians, data scientists, and researchers

RStudio: User Interface

title: Introduction to R
text:
Why Use R

Extensive libraries for data analysis and visualization

Active community support

Cross-platform compatibility (Windows, MacOS, Linux)

Integration with Python and C++

Free and open-source

title: Introduction to R
text:
Key Features of R

Comprehensive statistical analysis tools

Advanced graphics capabilities with ggplot2

Rich ecosystem of packages (dplyr, tidyr)

Interactive and reproducible research with RMarkdown or Quarto

title: Introduction to R
text:
R vs Python


R

Designed for statistical analysis and visualization

Rich ecosystem: dplyr, ggplot2, caret

Preferred in academia and research



Python

General-purpose language

Strong in data science and ML: pandas, scikit-learn, TensorFlow

Versatile for web, automation, and more

R: CRAN Windows

R: CRAN MacOS

RStudio: RStudio Desktop - Posit

Project

Centralized Management

Consistent Environment

Version Control Integration

Quicker Setup

title: Introduction to R
text:
Project: why not setwd()?

A Project (.Rproj) makes its own folder the working directory every time you open it
Paths are then relative to the project: read_csv("data/ncd_survey.csv") works on any computer
setwd("C:/Users/Asha/Desktop") only works on one machine, and breaks when you share the script
Keep raw data in data/, write all steps in a script (not only the console), and never overwrite the raw file

title: Introduction to R
text: Global options

title: Introduction to R
text:
New File — Core R Authoring

R Script — plain R code file for scripts and functions
R Notebook — interactive notebook with code, output, and narrative
R Markdown — reproducible reports combining R and text
Quarto Document — modern multi-language document format for reports
Quarto Presentation — slide decks built from Quarto content

title: Introduction to R
text:
New File — Documentation & Static Content

R HTML — HTML pages generated from R code and content
R Documentation — help files for packages and functions
Text File — plain text for notes, configs, or simple drafts

title: Introduction to R
text:
New File — Other Languages & Tools

Python Script — Python code file for reticulate and Python work
C++ File — C++ source for Rcpp or performance-critical code
SQL Script — SQL queries and database interactions
Stan File — Stan model code for Bayesian modeling
D3 Script — D3 JavaScript visualizations
R Sweave — LaTeX+R documents for PDF reporting
Shiny Web App — interactive apps built with Shiny
Plumber API — R APIs exposed as web services

title: Introduction to R
text:
Variables and Data Types

Numeric — numbers such as 3.14, 42
Integer — whole numbers with L suffix, e.g. 5L
Character — text values like "data"
Logical — TRUE or FALSE
Factor — categorical values with levels
Complex — numbers with imaginary parts like 1 + 2i



Show the code
x <- 5          # numeric
name <- "Alice" # character
flag <- TRUE    # logical
colors <- factor(c("red", "blue", "green"))



Variables store values in memory and can be reused later
R is dynamically typed: type depends on the stored value

title: Introduction to R
text:
Vectors and Sequences

Create ordered collections with c() and sequences with seq()
Useful for numeric data, indexes, and repeated values



Show the code
ages <- c(23, 35, 28)
seq(1, 100, 3)
seq(1, 2, length.out = 10)

title: Introduction to R
text:
Factors and Categorical Variables

Store categories or groups with fixed levels
Important for statistical modeling and reporting
Use factor() to make discrete labels or ordered categories



Show the code
gender <- factor(c("Male", "Female", "Male", "Female"),
                 levels = c("Male", "Female"))
physical_activity <- factor(sample(c(1, 2), 10, replace = TRUE),
                            levels = c(1, 2),
                            labels = c("Yes", "No"))

title: Introduction to R
section: Factor levels and the reference level
text:
Factor levels and the reference level


Show the code
res <- factor(c("Urban", "Rural", "Urban"))
levels(res)        # sorted alphabetically by default: "Rural" "Urban"


[1] "Rural" "Urban"



Unless you set levels = yourself, R sorts levels alphabetically; the first level is the reference in models
Choose it deliberately: factor(x, levels = c("Urban", "Rural"))
Text in quotes is a character, not a number: mean(c("45", "52")) fails. Convert with as.numeric()

title: Introduction to R
text:
Missing values spread


Show the code
wt <- c(60, 72, NA, 58)
mean(wt)                  # NA: one unknown value makes the mean unknown


[1] NA


Show the code
mean(wt, na.rm = TRUE)    # drop the missing value for this calculation (and report it)


[1] 63.33333

title: Introduction to R
text:
Lists and Matrices


Lists

Store mixed types in one object
Can contain vectors, data frames, functions, or other lists
Good for nested results and complex outputs



Show the code
my_list <- list(name = "Alice", score = 95, data = c(1, 2, 3))



Matrices

Two-dimensional arrays with a single data type
Ideal for numeric calculations, matrices, and linear algebra
Built from vectors using matrix(), cbind(), or rbind()



Show the code
m <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3)

title: Introduction to R
text:
Data Structures

Data frames are the most common table structure in R
They combine columns of equal length and can contain different types
Lists and matrices are also important foundational structures



Show the code
my_data <- data.frame(
  ID = 1:5,
  Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "David", "Eva"),
  Age = sample(20:50, 5, replace = TRUE)
)

title: Introduction to R
Introduction to R
text:
Packages

Collections of functions, data, and compiled code

title: Merging Datasets
text:
This module explains how to combine datasets by rows, columns, and with joins.



data1 <- data.frame(ID = 1:3, Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"), Age = c(23, 35, 28))
data2 <- data.frame(ID = 4:6, Name = c("David", "Eva", "Frank"), Age = c(45, 30, 40))
merged_rows <- rbind(data1, data2)
merged_rows

  ID    Name Age
1  1   Alice  23
2  2     Bob  35
3  3 Charlie  28
4  4   David  45
5  5     Eva  30
6  6   Frank  40






data1 <- data.frame(ID = 1:3, Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"))
data2 <- data.frame(Age = c(23, 35, 28), Height = c(165, 180, 175))
merged_columns <- cbind(data1, data2)
merged_columns

  ID    Name Age Height
1  1   Alice  23    165
2  2     Bob  35    180
3  3 Charlie  28    175






library(dplyr)


Attaching package: 'dplyr'


The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

    filter, lag


The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

data1 <- data.frame(
  ID = 1:5,
  Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "David", "Eva")
)
data2 <- data.frame(
  ID = c(2, 3, 5, 6),
  Score = c(85, 90, 88, 92)
)

inner_join(data1, data2, by = "ID")

  ID    Name Score
1  2     Bob    85
2  3 Charlie    90
3  5     Eva    88

left_join(data1, data2, by = "ID")

  ID    Name Score
1  1   Alice    NA
2  2     Bob    85
3  3 Charlie    90
4  4   David    NA
5  5     Eva    88

right_join(data1, data2, by = "ID")

  ID    Name Score
1  2     Bob    85
2  3 Charlie    90
3  5     Eva    88
4  6    <NA>    92

full_join(data1, data2, by = "ID")

  ID    Name Score
1  1   Alice    NA
2  2     Bob    85
3  3 Charlie    90
4  4   David    NA
5  5     Eva    88
6  6    <NA>    92


These join types are useful for combining medical records, survey forms, and measurement datasets.



bind_rows() (dplyr) does the same job as rbind(): tables with the same columns, different people.

library(dplyr)
round1 <- data.frame(id = 1:3, sbp = c(120, 135, 142))
round2 <- data.frame(id = 4:6, sbp = c(128, 150, 118))
bind_rows(round1, round2)

  id sbp
1  1 120
2  2 135
3  3 142
4  4 128
5  5 150
6  6 118





cbind() pastes by position and never checks who is who. If the two tables are sorted differently, the columns are silently mixed up. Join by a key such as id instead.




patients <- data.frame(id = 1:5, name = c("Asha", "Bina", "Chetan", "Dev", "Esha"))
labs     <- data.frame(id = c(3, 3, 5), hba1c = c(7.1, 6.8, 8.0))   # id 3 was tested twice
nrow(patients)

[1] 5

nrow(left_join(patients, labs, by = "id"))   # 6: patient 3 appears twice

[1] 6

count(labs, id)                                # check the key before joining

  id n
1  3 2
2  5 1


A left join keeps every patient, but a patient who matches two lab rows appears twice. Count rows before and after every join, and check that the key is unique in the table you join to.

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
What is Grammar of Graphics?

A systematic framework for creating visualizations
Developed by Leland Wilkinson, implemented in ggplot2 by Hadley Wickham
Treats plots as layered compositions of graphical elements
Separates data from aesthetics from geometry
Enables infinite combinations from finite components
More flexible than traditional plotting systems


Core Philosophy: Build complex visualizations by combining simple, well-defined layers

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
Why ggplot2?

Consistent syntax across all plot types
Flexible and extensible - easy to customize
Professional quality output
Reproducible - code-based approach
Large ecosystem of extensions
Industry standard in R community


vs Base R: More intuitive, consistent, and powerful for complex visualizations

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
The Seven Layers of Grammar

Data - The dataset being visualized
Aesthetics - Mapping data to visual properties
Geometries - Visual marks (points, lines, bars)
Statistics - Data transformations and summaries
Coordinates - The plotting space and axes
Facets - Subplots for data subsets
Scales - Mapping data values to aesthetics


Plus: Themes for overall visual styling

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
1. Data Layer
The foundation of every ggplot2 visualization

Must be a data frame or tibble
Each row represents an observation
Each column represents a variable
Data should be in tidy format

Each variable in one column
Each observation in one row
Each value in one cell




Code
# Basic structure
ggplot(data = my_data)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
2. Aesthetics (aes)
Mapping data variables to visual properties

Position: x, y
Color: color (points/lines), fill (areas)
Size: size of points or line width
Shape: point shapes
Transparency: alpha (0 = transparent, 1 = opaque)
Line type: linetype (solid, dashed, dotted)
Group: group (for grouping data)



Code
ggplot(data, aes(x = var1, y = var2, color = var3))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
3. Geometries (geom)
Visual representations of data

geom_point() - Scatter plots
geom_line() - Line graphs
geom_bar() / geom_col() - Bar charts
geom_histogram() - Histograms
geom_boxplot() - Box plots
geom_violin() - Violin plots
geom_smooth() - Smoothed conditional means
And many more…


Key concept: Geoms are added as layers with +

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
4. Statistics (stat)
Data transformations and summaries

Many geoms have default statistics
stat_identity - Use data as-is
stat_count - Count observations
stat_bin - Bin data into groups
stat_smooth - Add smoothed line
stat_summary - Compute summary statistics


Usually implicit: Most geoms automatically apply appropriate statistics

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
5. Coordinates (coord)
Defining the plotting space

coord_cartesian() - Default Cartesian coordinates
coord_flip() - Flip x and y axes
coord_polar() - Polar coordinates
coord_fixed() - Fixed aspect ratio
coord_trans() - Transformed coordinates



Code
# Flip axes for horizontal bars
ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
6. Facets
Creating subplots for data subsets

facet_wrap() - Wrap panels by one variable
facet_grid() - Grid of panels by two variables
Useful for comparing groups
Can have free or fixed scales



Code
# Facet by one variable
facet_wrap(~ treatment_group)

# Facet by two variables
facet_grid(gender ~ region)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
7. Scales
Mapping data values to aesthetic properties

Control how data maps to aesthetics
scale_x_continuous() - Continuous x-axis
scale_color_manual() - Manual color specification
scale_fill_brewer() - ColorBrewer palettes
scale_y_log10() - Logarithmic transformation
Control breaks, limits, labels, transformations



Code
scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue", "green"))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
8. Guides (Legends & Axes)
Helping readers interpret the plot

Axes: Show scale of position aesthetics
Legends: Show scale of other aesthetics (color, size, shape)
Controlled by guides() function
Can be positioned, styled, or removed
Automatically generated from aesthetics



Code
guides(color = guide_legend(title = "Treatment Group"))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
Building Plots Progressively
The power of layering

ggplot(data, aes(x = age, y = systolic_bp)) +        # 1. Data + aesthetics
  geom_point() +                                       # 2. Add points
  geom_smooth() +                                      # 3. Add trend line
  facet_wrap(~ treatment_group) +                      # 4. Add facets
  theme_minimal()                                      # 5. Apply theme


Each layer builds on the previous, creating complex visualizations from simple components

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
Data Preparation

# Create derived variables
bp_data <- bp_data %>%
  mutate(
    # BP change from baseline to 6 months
    SysBP_Change = SysBP_6m - SysBP_0m,
    DiaBP_Change = DiaBP_6m - DiaBP_0m,
    
    # Age groups
    AgeGroup = cut(Age, 
                   breaks = c(0, 30, 50, 65, 100),
                   labels = c("18-30", "31-50", "51-65", "65+")),
    
    # Hypertension status (Systolic ≥140 or Diastolic ≥90)
    Hypertension_Baseline = ifelse(SysBP_0m >= 140 | DiaBP_0m >= 90, 
                                   "Hypertensive", "Normal"),
    
    # BMI categories
    BMI_Category = cut(BMI,
                       breaks = c(0, 18.5, 25, 30, 100),
                       labels = c("Underweight", "Normal", "Overweight", "Obese"))
  )

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
Handling Missing Data

# Check missing data
missing_summary <- bp_data %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.))))

# Display columns with missing data
missing_summary %>%
  select(where(~. > 0))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  ExerciseFreq ChronicDisease
         <int>          <int>
1            2              2



Key variables with missing data: ExerciseFreq (44), ChronicDisease (75)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
Handling Missing Data: Strategies

# Strategy 1: Filter complete cases for specific analysis
bp_complete <- bp_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(ExerciseFreq), !is.na(ChronicDisease))

# Strategy 2: Use na.rm in calculations
bp_data %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP_0m, na.rm = TRUE))

# Strategy 3: Explicitly show missing as category
bp_data %>%
  mutate(ExerciseFreq = replace_na(ExerciseFreq, "Unknown"))

bp_time <- bp_data %>%
  select(PatientID, TreatmentGroup, SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m, SysBP_6m) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("SysBP"),
               names_to = "Time", values_to = "SysBP") %>%
  mutate(Months = as.numeric(gsub("SysBP_|m", "", Time)))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1

geom_line(): Time Series Code


Code
# Average BP over time by treatment
bp_summary <- bp_time %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup, Months) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(bp_summary, aes(x = Months, y = Mean_SysBP, 
                       color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5)



Use for: Showing trends over time or ordered categories
