Module 3 Overview
Previously: - Module 1: Foundations & Geoms - Module 2: Aesthetics & Faceting & Themes
This Module: - Color palettes & accessibility - paletteer package - Scale functions (manual, discrete, continuous, gradient) - Custom theme creation with theme() - element_text(), element_line(), element_rect(), element_blank() - Legend management

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
Setup


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readxl)
library(ggthemes)
library(paletteer)  # For extensive color palettes
library(patchwork)  # For combining plots

# Load data
bp_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx") %>%
  mutate(
    SysBP_Change = SysBP_6m - SysBP_0m,
    AgeGroup = cut(Age, breaks = c(0, 30, 50, 65, 100),
                   labels = c("18-30", "31-50", "51-65", "65+")),
    Hypertension_Baseline = ifelse(SysBP_0m >= 140 | DiaBP_0m >= 90, 
                                   "Hypertensive", "Normal"),
    BMI_Category = cut(BMI, breaks = c(0, 18.5, 25, 30, 100),
                       labels = c("Underweight", "Normal", "Overweight", "Obese"))
  )

region_summary <- bp_data %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP_0m), N = n(), .groups = "drop")

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
Color Theory Basics

Hue: The color itself (red, blue, green)
Saturation: Intensity/purity of color
Luminance: Brightness/lightness
Contrast: Difference between colors


Key principles: - Use color purposefully, not decoratively - Ensure sufficient contrast for readability - Consider colorblind accessibility (~8% of males, ~0.5% of females) - Limit number of colors (typically ≤7 for categorical data)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
scale_color_brewer() - ColorBrewer Palettes




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,
           color = Region)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
Best Practices for Color

Use color purposefully - not just for decoration
Prefer colorblind-safe palettes - viridis, ColorBrewer, paletteer curated sets
Limit colors - typically ≤7 distinct colors for categorical
Use redundant encoding - combine color with shape, pattern, or position
Ensure contrast - especially for text and important distinctions
Consider grayscale - will it work if printed in black & white?
Cultural context - red/green may have different meanings
Test with target audience - especially for accessibility needs

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
Creating an Organizational Theme


Code
# Hospital/Clinical Report Theme
theme_clinical_report <- function(base_size = 12, base_family = "serif") {
  theme_bw(base_size = base_size, base_family = base_family) +
  theme(
    # Professional serif fonts
    text = element_text(family = base_family),
    
    # Plot titles - centered and bold
    plot.title = element_text(size = base_size * 1.3, face = "bold", 
                              hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = base_size * 1.1, hjust = 0.5,
                                 color = "gray30", margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9, hjust = 1,
                                face = "italic", color = "gray50"),
    
    # Axis elements - clear and readable
    axis.title = element_text(size = base_size * 1.1, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9, color = "gray20"),
    axis.line = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    
    # Panel - clean with subtle grid
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "gray90", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "gray40", fill = NA, linewidth = 1),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    
    # Legend - bottom position, horizontal
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(size = base_size, face = "bold"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    legend.key = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    
    # Plot background
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
  )
}

Setup

title: Data Analysis
text:
Importance of Data Analysis


Making Sense of Data

Driving Informed Decisions — strategic choices based on evidence, not intuition
Identifying Patterns and Insights — uncovering hidden relationships in data
Optimizing Processes — streamline operations using performance metrics
Supporting Innovation — fuel new ideas and solutions


Research Perspective

Evidence-Based Research — validate hypotheses and draw reliable conclusions
Mitigating Risk — identify potential errors before they reach conclusions
Improving Reproducibility — ensures findings can be replicated
Ethical Responsibility — especially critical in clinical and health research

title: Data Analysis
text:
Why Test Selection Matters
Choosing the wrong test leads to Type I (false positive) or Type II (false negative) errors.







Reason
Detail




Accuracy & Validity
Test must match data nature and research question


Avoiding Errors
Wrong test → misleading conclusions


Reproducibility
Correct test ensures others can replicate findings


Meeting Objectives
Test must align with the hypothesis


Ethical Responsibility
In clinical research, conclusions affect real policy

title: Data Analysis
text:
Decision Framework — Overview

The choice of statistical test depends on: variable type → number of groups → normality → independence of observations







Note


Flowchart placeholder
Insert here: Overall test selection flowchart — starting from variable type (Categorical vs Continuous), then branching by number of groups, then normality, then paired vs unpaired.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Types of Variables






Note


Flowchart placeholder
Insert here: Variable classification diagram — Qualitative (Nominal, Ordinal) and Quantitative (Discrete, Continuous). Can also show examples relevant to your dataset such as sex, wealth index, age, SBP, FBS.





Categorical / Qualitative

Nominal — no order (e.g., sex, past history of DM)
Ordinal — ordered categories (e.g., wealth index: poorest → richest)
Binary / Dichotomous — two categories (e.g., screened: Yes/No)


Numerical / Quantitative

Discrete — whole numbers (e.g., number of visits)
Continuous — any value in a range (e.g., age, SBP, height, FBS)

title: Data Analysis
text:
Why Check Normality?
Many parametric tests (t-test, ANOVA, Pearson’s r) assume normally distributed data.
Failing to check normality can lead to:

Invalid p-values
Wrong test selection
Misleading conclusions

Two approaches: Visual methods + Statistical tests

title: Data Analysis
text:
Visual Methods — Histogram

hist(
  p$age_of_participants,
  main  = "Histogram with Density Line",
  xlab  = "Age",
  ylab  = "Density",
  col   = "grey",
  border = "black",
  freq  = FALSE
)
lines(density(p$age_of_participants), col = "red", lwd = 2)


A roughly bell-shaped curve suggests normality. Skewed or multimodal histograms indicate non-normality.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Visual Methods — QQ Plot

qqnorm(p$sbp_in_mm_hg, main = "Q-Q Plot: SBP")
qqline(p$sbp_in_mm_hg, col = "red")


Points should follow the red diagonal line closely if the data are normally distributed. Deviations at the tails indicate non-normality.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Statistical Tests — Shapiro-Wilk
Best for small samples (n ≤ 50). Randomly sample if n > 50.

p1 <- p[sample(nrow(p), 50), ]
s_test <- shapiro.test(p1$age_of_participants)
s_test


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  p1$age_of_participants
W = 0.95857, p-value = 0.07744



Interpretation: p > 0.05 → data does not significantly deviate from normality (cannot reject H₀ of normality).

title: Data Analysis
text:
Statistical Tests — Kolmogorov-Smirnov
Suitable for larger samples. Compares distribution to a theoretical normal.

ks_test <- ks.test(p$sbp_in_mm_hg, "pnorm",
                   mean = mean(p$sbp_in_mm_hg),
                   sd   = sd(p$sbp_in_mm_hg))
ks_test


    Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  p$sbp_in_mm_hg
D = 0.052082, p-value = 0.06522

title: Data Analysis
text:
Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit — 1 Group
Tests whether the observed distribution matches an expected distribution.

observed <- table(p$ever_screened_for_bp)
total    <- sum(observed)
expected <- c(1/2, 1/2) * total

chisq_test <- chisq.test(x = observed, p = expected / sum(expected))
chisq_test


    Chi-squared test for given probabilities

data:  observed
X-squared = 80.23, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16



Assumption: Expected frequency ≥ 5 in each cell.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Chi-Square Test — 2 Binary Groups (Expected ≥ 5)
Tests association between two categorical variables using a contingency table.

table_gender_dm <- table(p$sex_of_participants, p$past_history_of_diabetes)
table_gender_dm

        
          no yes
  female 332  17
  male   265  17

chisq_m5

chisq_m5$expected

  female 330.1949 18.80507
  male   266.8051 15.19493



Use correct = FALSE to apply the standard Pearson Chi-square (no Yates correction).

title: Data Analysis
text:
Chi-Square — Yates Continuity Correction
Yates correction subtracts 0.5 from the absolute difference between observed and expected frequency before squaring.

# With Yates correction (correct = TRUE is default for 2x2 tables)

title: Data Analysis
text:
One Group — Z Test
Use when population SD is known and n > 30.

pr  <- p |> filter(wealth_index_of_participants == "richer")
mu  <- mean(p$age_of_participants)
sigma <- sd(p$age_of_participants)

s_mean <- mean(pr$age_of_participants)
n      <- length(pr$age_of_participants)
z      <- (s_mean - mu) / (sigma / sqrt(n))

p_two_tailed     <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z)))
p_one_tailed_gt  <- 1 - pnorm(z)
p_one_tailed_lt  <- pnorm(z)

cat("Z =", round(z, 3),
    "\nTwo-tailed p =", round(p_two_tailed, 4),
    "\nOne-tailed (greater) p =", round(p_one_tailed_gt, 4))

Z = -0.879 
Two-tailed p = 0.3794 
One-tailed (greater) p = 0.8103

This section covers common statistical tests used in medical research, implemented in R.



# Load necessary libraries
library(tidyverse)

✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0

✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

library(gtsummary)

# Example data
data <- data.frame(
  age = rnorm(100, 50, 10),
  blood_pressure = rnorm(100, 120, 15),
  treatment = sample(c("A", "B"), 100, replace = TRUE)
)

# Summary statistics
data %>% 
  tbl_summary()











Characteristic
N = 1001




age
50 (43, 56)


blood_pressure
121 (111, 132)


treatment




    A
44 (44%)


    B
56 (56%)



1 Median (Q1, Q3); n (%)














# Two-sample t-test
t.test(blood_pressure ~ treatment, data = data)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  blood_pressure by treatment
t = -1.3721, df = 94.534, p-value = 0.1733
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group A and group B is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -10.781784   1.969399
sample estimates:
mean in group A mean in group B 
       117.6492        122.0554 






# Create categorical data
data$outcome <- sample(c("Improved", "Not Improved"), 100, replace = TRUE)

# Chi-square test
chisq.test(table(data$treatment, data$outcome))


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  table(data$treatment, data$outcome)
X-squared = 0.014758, df = 1, p-value = 0.9033













Outcome
Groups / predictor
Usual test




Continuous
2 independent groups
Two-sample (Welch) t-test


Continuous
same people measured twice (before/after)
Paired t-test


Continuous, skewed or small sample
2 independent groups
Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney)


Continuous
3 or more groups
One-way ANOVA (Kruskal-Wallis if skewed)


Categorical (yes/no)
categorical
Chi-square test (Fisher’s exact if expected counts are small)







t.test(blood_pressure ~ treatment, data = data)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  blood_pressure by treatment
t = -1.3721, df = 94.534, p-value = 0.1733
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group A and group B is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -10.781784   1.969399
sample estimates:
mean in group A mean in group B 
       117.6492        122.0554 



R uses Welch’s t-test by default (does not assume equal variances).
The confidence interval is for the first group minus the second (A − B), so the sign follows the order of the groups.
The sample estimates show each group’s mean.





# paired: the same 30 people before and after
before <- rnorm(30, 140, 12)
after  <- before - rnorm(30, 5, 6)
t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE)


    Paired t-test

data:  before and after
t = 1.4842, df = 29, p-value = 0.1485
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.8405802  5.2883927
sample estimates:
mean difference 
       2.223906 

# non-parametric alternative for two independent groups
wilcox.test(blood_pressure ~ treatment, data = data)


    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  blood_pressure by treatment
W = 1027, p-value = 0.1556
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0






A p-value says how surprising the data would be if there were no true difference.
It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and not the probability the result is “due to chance”.
It says nothing about the size or importance of the difference: look at the estimate and its confidence interval.
A large p-value is weak evidence against “no difference”. It is not proof that there is none.





Regression modeling now has its own dedicated module — see Regression Analysis for simple/multiple regression, diagnostics, and logistic regression.

X-squared = 0.014758, df = 1, p-value = 0.9033













Outcome
Groups / predictor
Usual test




Continuous
2 independent groups
Two-sample (Welch) t-test


Continuous
same people measured twice (before/after)
Paired t-test


Continuous, skewed or small sample
2 independent groups
Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney)


Continuous
3 or more groups
One-way ANOVA (Kruskal-Wallis if skewed)


Categorical (yes/no)
categorical
Chi-square test (Fisher’s exact if expected counts are small)







t.test(blood_pressure ~ treatment, data = data)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  blood_pressure by treatment
t = -1.3721, df = 94.534, p-value = 0.1733
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group A and group B is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -10.781784   1.969399
sample estimates:
mean in group A mean in group B 
       117.6492        122.0554 



R uses Welch’s t-test by default (does not assume equal variances).
The confidence interval is for the first group minus the second (A − B), so the sign follows the order of the groups.
The sample estimates show each group’s mean.





# paired: the same 30 people before and after
before <- rnorm(30, 140, 12)
after  <- before - rnorm(30, 5, 6)
t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE)


    Paired t-test

data:  before and after
t = 1.4842, df = 29, p-value = 0.1485
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.8405802  5.2883927
sample estimates:
mean difference 
       2.223906 

# non-parametric alternative for two independent groups
wilcox.test(blood_pressure ~ treatment, data = data)


    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  blood_pressure by treatment
W = 1027, p-value = 0.1556
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0






A p-value says how surprising the data would be if there were no true difference.
It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and not the probability the result is “due to chance”.
It says nothing about the size or importance of the difference: look at the estimate and its confidence interval.
A large p-value is weak evidence against “no difference”. It is not proof that there is none.

title: Debugging Plots
text:
Debugging plots are essential tools for diagnosing issues in data visualization and analysis. They help identify problems such as incorrect data representation, scaling issues, or unexpected patterns in the data. In this guide, we will explore various techniques and tools for creating effective debugging plots.





Missing or incorrect data types
# Check data types
str(mtcars)

# Check for missing values
sum(is.na(mtcars))

# Visualize missing patterns
library(naniar)
vis_miss(mtcars)
Outliers affecting scales
# Check for outliers
boxplot(mtcars$mpg)

# Use robust statistics
library(robustbase)
summary(mtcars$mpg)





Mapping vs Setting Aesthetics
# Correct: Map color to variable
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point()

# Incorrect: Setting color globally
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = "red")  # This sets all points to red
Factor Level Issues
# Check factor levels
levels(mtcars$cyl)

# Reorder factors if needed
mtcars$cyl <- factor(mtcars$cyl, levels = c("4", "6", "8"))
Geom Conflicts
# Error: Can't use geom_bar with y aesthetic
# ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) + geom_bar()

# Correct: Use stat = "identity"
ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "identity")







# Check ggplot object structure
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
str(p)

# View plot data
p$data
p$mapping



# Build plot incrementally
p1 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg))
print(p1)  # Should show empty plot

p2 <- p1 + geom_point()
print(p2)  # Check if points appear

p3 <- p2 + theme_minimal()
print(p3)  # Check theme application



# Enable ggplot2 debugging
options(ggplot2.debug = TRUE)

# Check for warnings
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()






# Problem: Length mismatch
# ggplot(data, aes(x = x_var, y = y_var, color = short_vector))

# Solution: Ensure vectors are same length or use single values
ggplot(data, aes(x = x_var, y = y_var, color = factor(category)))



# Problem: Wrong scale type
# ggplot(data, aes(x = factor_var, y = numeric_var)) + scale_x_continuous()

# Solution: Use appropriate scale
ggplot(data, aes(x = factor_var, y = numeric_var)) + scale_x_discrete()



# Problem: Typo in parameter name
# geom_point(size = 3)  # Correct
# geom_point(siz = 3)   # Incorrect

# Solution: Check documentation
?geom_point






# Residual plots for model diagnostics
model <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
plot(model)

# QQ plots for normality
qqnorm(mtcars$mpg)
qqline(mtcars$mpg)



# Correlation plots
library(corrplot)
corrplot(cor(mtcars))

# Pairs plots
pairs(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp")])



# Plot data distributions
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg)) + 
  geom_histogram() + 
  facet_wrap(~ cyl)

# Check for data issues
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_text(aes(label = rownames(mtcars)), check_overlap = TRUE)






# When plot fails
tryCatch({
  ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
}, error = function(e) {
  print(e)
  traceback()
})



library(profvis)

# Profile plotting code
profvis({
  p <- ggplot(large_dataset, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point()
  print(p)
})



# Check memory usage
gc()

# For large datasets, use sampling
sample_data <- mtcars[sample(nrow(mtcars), 1000, replace = TRUE), ]
ggplot(sample_data, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()





Start simple: Build plots incrementally
Check data first: Validate input data before plotting
Use reproducible examples: Create minimal examples that reproduce issues
Read error messages carefully: They often point to the exact problem
Check package versions: Ensure compatible versions of ggplot2 and extensions
Use debugging tools: Leverage R’s debugging functions and ggplot2’s debug options
Document fixes: Keep notes on solutions for future reference

title: Plotting Tools
text:
This chapter introduces various tools and libraries available in R for creating visualizations. It covers base R plotting functions, as well as popular packages like ggplot2 and lattice, which offer advanced capabilities for creating complex and customizable plots.


R’s built-in plotting functions provide a solid foundation for data visualization:


# Scatter plot
plot(x = mtcars$wt, y = mtcars$mpg,
     xlab = "Weight", ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
     main = "Scatter Plot Example")

# Line plot
plot(x = 1:10, y = (1:10)^2, type = "l",
     xlab = "X", ylab = "Y^2")

# Bar plot
barplot(height = c(10, 15, 8, 12),
        names.arg = c("A", "B", "C", "D"))

# Histogram
hist(mtcars$mpg, breaks = 10,
     xlab = "Miles per Gallon",
     main = "Histogram of MPG")



# Multiple plots in one window
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))  # 2x2 grid

plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
hist(mtcars$mpg)
boxplot(mtcars$mpg ~ mtcars$cyl)
plot(density(mtcars$mpg))

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))  # Reset to single plot




ggplot2 is the most popular R package for data visualization, based on the Grammar of Graphics:


library(ggplot2)

# Basic scatter plot
ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point()

# Adding aesthetics
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "MPG vs Weight by Cylinders",
       x = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
       y = "Miles per Gallon")



# Points, lines, bars
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg))

p + geom_point()           # Scatter plot
p + geom_smooth()          # Smooth line
p + geom_line()            # Line plot
p + geom_bar(stat = "identity")  # Bar plot
p + geom_histogram()       # Histogram
p + geom_boxplot()         # Box plot



# Faceting
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ cyl) +
  theme_minimal()

# Custom themes
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("Custom Theme Example")




Lattice provides trellis graphics for multivariate data:
library(lattice)

# Scatter plot matrix
splom(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp")])

# Conditional plots
xyplot(mpg ~ wt | factor(cyl), data = mtcars,
       layout = c(3, 1))

# 3D plots
cloud(mpg ~ wt * hp, data = mtcars)





library(plotly)

# Convert ggplot to interactive
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
ggplotly(p)

# Native plotly
plot_ly(mtcars, x = ~wt, y = ~mpg, type = "scatter", mode = "markers")



library(ggvis)

# Interactive ggplot2-like syntax
mtcars %>%
  ggvis(x = ~wt, y = ~mpg) %>%
  layer_points() %>%
  add_tooltip(function(df) paste("Weight:", df$wt, "MPG:", df$mpg))






library(ggstatsplot)

# Statistical plots with tests
ggbetweenstats(data = mtcars, x = cyl, y = mpg)



library(ggplot2)
library(maps)

# Basic map
world <- map_data("world")
ggplot(world, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = "lightblue", color = "black")



library(igraph)
library(ggraph)

# Create network
g <- make_ring(10)
ggraph(g, layout = "circle") +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point(size = 5)





Base R: Quick plots, statistical graphics
ggplot2: Publication-quality static plots, complex customizations
Lattice: Multivariate data, trellis displays
plotly/ggvis: Interactive web-based visualizations
Specialized packages: Domain-specific visualizations (maps, networks, etc.)





Know your data: Choose plot types that best represent your data
Keep it simple: Avoid clutter, focus on the message
Use color effectively: Consider colorblind-friendly palettes
Label clearly: Include informative titles, axis labels, legends
Test different tools: Experiment with different packages for the best result

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggstatsplot is an R package that combines statistical tests and publication-ready visualisations in a single function call. Each plot automatically selects, runs, and annotates the appropriate statistical test based on your data, displaying results directly on the figure.
This removes a common workflow bottleneck: running a test in one place, building a plot in another, and manually annotating results.

install.packages("ggstatsplot")
library(ggstatsplot)

Why use it?

One function produces both the visual and the statistical result
Automatically annotates effect sizes and confidence intervals
Sensible defaults — works out of the box for most common comparisons
Output is a ggplot2 object, so you can add layers or themes as usual

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
section: Core functions covered in this module
text:
Core functions covered in this module



Function
Use case




ggbetweenstats()
Compare groups (independent samples)


ggscatterstats()
Correlation between two continuous variables


gghistostats()
Distribution of a single continuous variable

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggbetweenstats() — Group Comparisons
Use this when you want to compare a continuous variable across two or more independent groups.

library(ggstatsplot)

# Compare systolic BP across fuel type groups
ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,         # grouping variable (categorical)
  y     = sbp_0m,            # outcome variable (continuous)
  title = "Systolic BP by Fuel Type"
)

What the output shows:

A violin + boxplot combination with individual data points
The statistical test used (Welch’s ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis, chosen automatically)
The p-value, effect size (η² or ε²), and confidence interval
Pairwise comparisons (if more than 2 groups)

Choosing parametric vs non-parametric:

# Force non-parametric (Kruskal-Wallis)
ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  type  = "nonparametric"   # "parametric", "nonparametric", "robust", "bayes"
)

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggscatterstats() — Correlation
Use this when you want to examine the relationship between two continuous variables.

ggscatterstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = current_age,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  title = "Age vs Systolic BP at Baseline"
)

What the output shows:

A scatter plot with a linear trend line and confidence band
Pearson (or Spearman) correlation coefficient, r
p-value and 95% confidence interval for r
Marginal histograms on both axes

Using Spearman instead of Pearson:

ggscatterstats(
  data = overall_up,
  x    = current_age,
  y    = sbp_0m,
  type = "nonparametric"   # uses Spearman's rho
)

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
gghistostats() — Distribution
Use this when you want to visualise the distribution of a single continuous variable with a one-sample test.

gghistostats(
  data     = overall_up,
  x        = current_age,
  title    = "Distribution of Age at Enrolment",
  test.value = 40          # hypothesised population mean
)

What the output shows:

Histogram with overlaid density curve
One-sample t-test (or Wilcoxon signed-rank) against the specified test.value
Mean, median, and their confidence intervals

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
Reading the statistical annotation
Every ggstatsplot figure includes a subtitle with the test results in a standardised format:
Welch's ANOVA, F(2, 147.3) = 5.23, p = 0.006, ω² = 0.06, 95% CI [0.01, 0.14]



Component
Meaning




Test name
Which test was used (selected automatically)


Test statistic
F, t, χ², H etc.


p-value
Statistical significance


Effect size
Practical significance (ω², d, r, etc.)


95% CI
Uncertainty around the effect size









TipInterpreting effect sizes




η² / ω²: Small ≈ 0.01, Medium ≈ 0.06, Large ≈ 0.14 (for ANOVA)
Cohen’s d: Small ≈ 0.2, Medium ≈ 0.5, Large ≈ 0.8 (for t-tests)
r: Small ≈ 0.1, Medium ≈ 0.3, Large ≈ 0.5 (for correlation)

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
Quick reference

# Two-group comparison
ggbetweenstats(data = df, x = group, y = outcome)

# Correlation
ggscatterstats(data = df, x = var1, y = var2)

# Distribution
gghistostats(data = df, x = continuous_var, test.value = 0)

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Note



This module builds on Quarto Basics. It assumes you can create and render a .qmd file and write basic code chunks.

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
What you will learn

Parameterised reports — run the same document for different subgroups
Inline R code — embed values directly in prose
Cross-references for figures and tables
Multiple output formats from one source file
Integrating gtsummary tables in Quarto

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Parameterised Reports
Parameters let you run the same document with different inputs — for example, generating one report per hospital, intervention group, or region.

1. Declare parameters in the YAML header
---
title: "Site Report"
params:
  site_name: "Site A"
  intervention: "Control"
---


2. Use parameters in code

# params$site_name and params$intervention are available as R objects
site_data <- overall_up |>
  filter(site == params$site_name,
         intervention == params$intervention)

nrow(site_data)



3. Render with different parameter values

# Render from R for a specific site
quarto::quarto_render(
  input  = "site_report.qmd",
  output_file = "site_a_report.html",
  execute_params = list(
    site_name    = "Site A",
    intervention = "Intervention"
  )
)



4. Batch render — one file per site

library(purrr)

sites <- c("Site A", "Site B", "Site C")

walk(sites, \(site) {
  quarto::quarto_render(
    input          = "site_report.qmd",
    output_file    = paste0(tolower(gsub(" ", "_", site)), "_report.html"),
    execute_params = list(site_name = site)
  )
})

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Inline R Code
Embedding computed values directly in text avoids copy-paste errors and keeps your document reproducible.
Syntax:
200

# In a code chunk (runs silently):
n_total  <- nrow(overall_up)
mean_age <- round(mean(overall_up$current_age, na.rm = TRUE), 1)

In Quarto prose:
The study enrolled 200 participants with a mean age of
NA years (SD = 14.3).
Rendered output:

The study enrolled 1 248 participants with a mean age of 38.4 years (SD = 11.2).







Tip



Compute all summary values in one early code chunk marked #| include: false, then reference them via inline code throughout the document.

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Cross-References
Cross-references auto-number figures and tables and create clickable links.

Figures
Add a label that starts with fig- and a fig-cap:
```{r}
#| label: fig-sbp-hist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of baseline systolic blood pressure."
ggplot(overall_up, aes(x = sbp_0m)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(x = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", y = "Count")
```
Reference in text: @fig-sbp-hist → renders as “Figure 1”


Tables
Add a label starting with tbl- and a tbl-cap:
```{r}
#| label: tbl-demographics
#| tbl-cap: "Baseline characteristics of study participants."
library(gtsummary)
overall_up |>
  select(current_age, sex, tobacco_type, fuel_type) |>
  tbl_summary()
```
Reference in text: @tbl-demographics → renders as “Table 1”

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Multiple Output Formats
One .qmd file can produce HTML, PDF, and Word output.
---
title: "Study Report"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    theme: flatly
  pdf:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
  docx:
    toc: true
---
Render all formats at once:
quarto render study_report.qmd






WarningPDF requirements



PDF rendering requires a LaTeX installation. Install tinytex from R:
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Code Chunk Options Reference



Option
Effect




echo: false
Hide code, show output


include: false
Run code silently (no output shown)


eval: false
Show code but don’t run it


warning: false
Suppress warnings


message: false
Suppress package messages


fig-width: 8
Figure width in inches


fig-height: 5
Figure height in inches


fig-dpi: 300
Resolution for saved figures



Set globally in YAML to apply to all chunks:
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false

title: Survival Analysis Cheat Sheet
text:
Item
Meaning




time
follow-up from time zero to the event or censoring (one unit)


status
1 = event, 0 = censored


censored
observed event-free up to a time, then unknown (alive at the end, lost to follow-up)


Surv(time, status)
the survival object; 17.2+ = censored at 17.2



Our cohort: 600 patients, 113 deaths (19%), 487 censored.











Question
Method
R




How is survival over time?
Kaplan-Meier
survfit(Surv(t, s) ~ 1)


Survival at 12 months?
KM at a time
summary(km, times = 12)


Do two or more curves differ?
Log-rank
survdiff(Surv(t, s) ~ g)


Effect size, adjusted for covariates
Cox regression
coxph(Surv(t, s) ~ x1 + x2)


Event rate per person-time
rate
events / sum(time) * 100


Typical follow-up
reverse KM
survfit(Surv(t, 1 - s) ~ 1)


Is the HR constant over time?
PH test
cox.zph(fit)













Result
How to say it




KM at 12 months: 0.83
“83% were alive 12 months after starting treatment (95% CI 80–86%)”


Median = NA
“median not reached”: fewer than half died; report survival at fixed times


Log-rank p
“survival differed (p = …)”: direction from observed vs expected


HR = exp(coef)
“at any time, the hazard is HR times that of the reference group”


HR for HIV: 1.80 (1.10–2.95)
“about 80% higher hazard of death in HIV-positive patients”


CI includes 1
no clear association



HR is a rate ratio, not a risk ratio. Rescale continuous variables (per 10 years, per 5 kg/m²).




Events per coefficient about 10 or more: here 14.1
Choose covariates from theory (not p-values); report crude and adjusted HRs and reference groups
Check PH: cox.zph() and a plot; one borderline term among many may be chance
If violated: strata() (nuisance factor), time-split (survSplit) to report the effect by period, or time-varying effects
Report with tbl_regression(fit, exponentiate = TRUE)






Mean of follow-up times or a t-test on them; proportion died when follow-up differs
Median replaced by the median of observed times when it is “not reached”
Reading the thin right tail of a KM curve; no number at risk
Informative censoring (the sickest are lost); competing risks ignored
Immortal time bias; different time zero in the groups
HR read as risk ratio; one HR reported when the effect changes over time
Too few events for the covariates; association read as cause





Of 600 patients (median follow-up 18 months by reverse Kaplan-Meier), 113 died and 487 were censored. Twelve-month survival was 83% (95% CI 80–86%). In a multivariable Cox model, HIV (HR 2.0) and MDR-TB (HR 2.1) were associated with a higher hazard of death and DOT with a lower hazard (HR 0.6); smear status violated proportional hazards and was stratified.

title: Session 2 — Kaplan-Meier Curves
text:
Where we are

Session 1: censoring, the Surv object, rates
Today: estimate and draw the survival curve without assuming a constant rate
By the end you can:

fit and read a Kaplan-Meier curve
report survival at a time point and the median (or “not reached”)
draw curves by group with a number-at-risk table

title: Session 2 — Kaplan-Meier Curves
text:
A step function
At each event time, survival drops by the fraction who die among those still at risk; censored patients leave the risk set without causing a drop.

S(t) = Π (1 − di / ni) over event times ≤ t


toy <- tibble(time = c(2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 8), status = c(1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1))
summary(survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, toy))

Call: survfit(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = toy)

 time n.risk n.event survival std.err lower 95% CI upper 95% CI
    2      6       1    0.833   0.152        0.583            1
    3      5       1    0.667   0.192        0.379            1
    5      3       1    0.444   0.222        0.167            1
    8      1       1    0.000     NaN           NA           NA

title: Session 2 — Kaplan-Meier Curves
text:
Reading the toy example

At time 2: 6 at risk, 1 dies: 1 × 5/6 = 0.83
At time 3: 5 at risk, 1 dies and 1 is censored: 0.83 × 4/5 = 0.67
The censored patient counts in the denominator until censored, then leaves

title: Session 2 — Kaplan-Meier Curves
text:
The overall curve

km <- survfit(Surv(time_months, status) ~ 1, data = tb)
km

Call: survfit(formula = Surv(time_months, status) ~ 1, data = tb)

       n events median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL
[1,] 600    113     NA      NA      NA



ggsurvfit(km) + add_confidence_interval() + labs(x = "Months since starting treatment", y = "Survival probability") + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.5, 1))

title: Session 2 — Kaplan-Meier Curves
text: The overall curve

title: Session 2 — Kaplan-Meier Curves
text:
Survival at a time

summary(km, times = c(6, 12, 18))

Call: survfit(formula = Surv(time_months, status) ~ 1, data = tb)

 time n.risk n.event survival std.err lower 95% CI upper 95% CI
    6    490      76    0.870  0.0140        0.843        0.897
   12    439      20    0.833  0.0156        0.803        0.864
   18    244      17    0.796  0.0173        0.763        0.831



“Survival at 12 months was 83% (95% CI 80–86%).” Time points beyond the longest follow-up (here about 24 months) cannot be estimated.

title: Session 2 — Kaplan-Meier Curves
text:
The median survival time

The median is the time at which the curve crosses 0.5
Here fewer than half the patients died, so the curve never reaches 0.5: the median is not reached (NA)
Report survival at fixed times (12, 24 months) or the restricted mean instead
Never replace “not reached” with the median of the observed times


summary(km)$table[c("records", "events", "median")]

records  events  median 
    600     113      NA

title: Session 2 — Kaplan-Meier Curves
text:
Confidence and the tail

The curve is least reliable at the right end, where few patients remain at risk: confidence bands widen and a single death moves the curve a lot. Always show the number at risk and avoid over-reading the tail.

title: Session 2 — Kaplan-Meier Curves
text:
HIV-positive and negative

km_grp <- survfit(Surv(time_months, status) ~ hiv, data = tb)
summary(km_grp, times = 12)$surv |> round(2)

[1] 0.85 0.72



ggsurvfit(km_grp) + add_confidence_interval() + add_risktable() + scale_ggsurvfit(x_scales = list(breaks = seq(0, 24, 6))) +
  labs(x = "Months since starting treatment", y = "Survival probability")



Positive patients have lower survival throughout
Overlapping bands early on; separation grows

title: Session 2 — Kaplan-Meier Curves

Self-check quiz (1/5)

In a Kaplan-Meier analysis the median survival time is reported as ‘not reached’. What does this mean?

The patients were followed for too short a time to be analysed
The median could not be calculated because of missing data in the file
Fewer than half of the patients had died by the end of follow-up
More than half of the patients in the whole cohort were censored

title: Session 2 — Kaplan-Meier Curves
text:
Self-check quiz (2/5)

What happens to a censored patient in the Kaplan-Meier calculation?

They are counted as a death at the time of censoring in the data
They stay at risk until censored, then leave with no drop
They are removed from the whole analysis from the very start of it
They are counted as surviving until the end of the study period

title: Session 2 — Kaplan-Meier Curves

Why should a Kaplan-Meier plot show the number at risk beneath the curve?

It gives the p-value for the comparison made between the two groups
It shows the hazard ratio for each one of the groups in the plot
The right end of the curve rests on few patients and is unreliable
It is included only to make the plot look more complete and tidy

At 12 months the Kaplan-Meier survival for HIV-positive patients is 0.72. How should this be stated?

The hazard of dying in the HIV-positive group is 0.72 per month of time
The median survival of HIV-positive patients is about 0.72 of a year

title: Session 4 — Cox Proportional Hazards Regression
text:
Where we are

Sessions 2–3: describe and compare curves
Today: regression for survival: effect sizes, adjustment for several variables
By the end you can:

fit a Cox model and interpret a hazard ratio and its CI

title: Session 4 — Cox Proportional Hazards Regression
text:
The model

h(t | x) = h0(t) × exp(β1x1 + β2x2 + …)


h0(t) is an unspecified baseline hazard: the shape over time is left free
exp(β) is the hazard ratio: the multiplicative change in the hazard for a one-unit increase in x, at any time
Proportional hazards: that ratio is constant over time (checked in Session 5)
Like logistic regression it uses exp(coefficient), but it models rates over time

title: Session 4 — Cox Proportional Hazards Regression
text:
One predictor

cox1 <- coxph(Surv(time_months, status) ~ hiv, data = tb)
exp(cbind(HR = coef(cox1), confint(cox1))) |> round(2)

             HR 2.5 % 97.5 %
hivPositive 1.8   1.1   2.95



HR = 1.8 (95% CI 1.1–2.9): at any time, the hazard of death is about 80% higher in HIV-positive patients. It is a rate ratio, not a risk ratio; and unlike the log-rank test it has a size and a CI.

text:
Several predictors at once

cox_full <- coxph(Surv(time_months, status) ~ age + sex + hiv + diabetes + smoker + bmi + mdr_tb + treatment, data = tb)
round(exp(cbind(HR = coef(cox_full), confint(cox_full))), 2)    # tbl_regression(cox_full, exponentiate = TRUE) formats this for a paper

               HR 2.5 % 97.5 %
age          1.01  1.00   1.03
sexMale      1.08  0.72   1.64
hivPositive  1.96  1.18   3.25
diabetesYes  1.37  0.69   2.75
smokerYes    1.10  0.73   1.66
bmi          0.92  0.86   0.98
mdr_tbYes    2.11  1.25   3.58
treatmentDOT 0.57  0.39   0.83

title: Session 4 — Cox Proportional Hazards Regression
text:
Reading the adjusted hazard ratios

Each HR is adjusted for the others: “holding age, sex, … fixed”
MDR-TB about doubles the hazard; DOT about halves it (reference: self-administered); sex shows no effect
The CI shows the precision: a CI that includes 1 means no clear association

title: Session 4 — Cox Proportional Hazards Regression
text:
Reading continuous predictors

cox_age10 <- coxph(Surv(time_months, status) ~ I(age / 10) + hiv + mdr_tb + treatment, data = tb)
round(exp(cbind(HR = coef(cox_age10), confint(cox_age10))), 2)[1, ]

    HR  2.5 % 97.5 % 
  1.16   1.01   1.33 


The HR for age is for one year unless you rescale: per 10 years is a more readable unit (HR^10). For BMI, use a clinically sensible step (per 5 kg/m²).

title: Session 4 — Cox Proportional Hazards Regression
text:
Events per variable

c(events = sum(tb$status), coefficients = length(coef(cox_full)), events_per_coefficient = round(sum(tb$status) / length(coef(cox_full)), 1))

                events           coefficients events_per_coefficient 
                 113.0                    8.0                   14.1 



The information in a Cox model is the number of events, not the number of patients. As a rule of thumb, aim for about 10 or more events per coefficient; with fewer, estimates are unstable and the model overfits. Choose predictors from theory first (Session 6 of the regression workshop).

Predicted survival for a patient profile

nd <- tibble(age = 40, sex = "Male", hiv = c("Negative", "Positive"), diabetes = "No", smoker = "No", bmi = 20, mdr_tb = "No", treatment = "DOT") |>
  mutate(across(c(sex, hiv, diabetes, smoker, mdr_tb, treatment), \(v) factor(v, levels = levels(tb[[cur_column()]]))))
ps <- survfit(cox_full, newdata = nd)
tibble(month = ps$time, hiv_neg = ps$surv[, 1], hiv_pos = ps$surv[, 2]) |> pivot_longer(-month, names_to = "profile", values_to = "survival") |>
  ggplot(aes(month, survival, colour = profile)) + geom_step(linewidth = 1) + labs(x = "Months", y = "Predicted survival", colour = NULL)

title: Session 2 — Poisson Regression
text:
Where we are

Session 1: counts, rates, person-time, the Poisson idea
Today: regression for counts and rates
By the end you can:

fit a Poisson regression and read rate ratios
use an offset so the model describes rates
adjust for rain, ward type, trend and season
predict expected counts

title: Session 2 — Poisson Regression
text:
A log-linear model

log(mu) = b0 + b1 x1 + b2 x2 + … so mu = exp(b0) x exp(b1)x1 x …


The log link keeps the expected count positive
exp(b) is a multiplicative effect on the mean: a rate ratio (or count ratio)
glm(y ~ x, family = poisson)
Like logistic regression, but the outcome is a count and exp(b) is a ratio of means/rates

title: Session 2 — Poisson Regression
text:
Why the offset?
Wards differ in population, so the expected count is proportional to population:

log(mu) = log(population) + b0 + b1 x1 (the offset: coefficient fixed at 1)


m0 <- glm(cases ~ fogging, family = poisson, data = dg)                                   # no offset: compares MEAN COUNTS
m1 <- glm(cases ~ fogging + offset(log(population)), family = poisson, data = dg)         # with offset: compares RATES
round(exp(cbind(no_offset = coef(m0), with_offset = coef(m1)))["foggingYes", ], 2)

  no_offset with_offset 
       0.83        0.86 



Without the offset the model compares mean counts per ward-month, mixing risk with population size. Use offset(log(person-time)) whenever groups differ in size or follow-up.

tbl_regression(m2, exponentiate = TRUE, include = c(fogging, slum, rain_lag1, month_index))

title: Session 4 — Excess Zeros and Model Checking
text:
Where we are

Session 3: overdispersion and the negative binomial
Today: too many zeros, and does the model fit?
By the end you can:

compare observed and expected zeros
tell structural from sampling zeros
fit and judge a zero-inflated model

title: Session 4 — Excess Zeros and Model Checking
text:
Are there too many?

m_nb <- MASS::glm.nb(cases ~ fogging + slum + rain_lag1 + month_index + sin(2 * pi * month / 12) + cos(2 * pi * month / 12) + offset(log(population)), data = dg)
c(observed = round(mean(dg$cases == 0), 3), nb_expected = round(mean(dnbinom(0, mu = fitted(m_nb), size = m_nb$theta)), 3))

   observed nb_expected 
      0.202       0.186 



A good negative binomial already allows many zeros: here it expects about 19% and 20% are observed, a small excess
More zeros than a count model expects needs an explanation, not automatically a new model

title: Session 4 — Excess Zeros and Model Checking
section: Where do the zeros come from?
text:
Where do the zeros come from?

dg |> group_by(ward) |> summarise(zero_months = sum(cases == 0), mean_cases = round(mean(cases), 1)) |> arrange(desc(zero_months)) |> head(6)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  ward  zero_months mean_cases
  <fct>       <int>      <dbl>
1 W14            24        0.9
2 W02            21        2.9
3 W04            18        4.1
4 W23            18       11.6
5 W12            16        3.9
6 W20            13        2.8



A few wards report zero for half of the months. That is not “no dengue”: it is weak surveillance. These are structural zeros (the count process is switched off), as opposed to sampling zeros (low mean, no case by chance).

title: Session 4 — Excess Zeros and Model Checking
text:
Two processes

P(Y = 0) = pi + (1 - pi) x Pcount(0) P(Y = k) = (1 - pi) x Pcount(k)


Zero-inflated: with probability pi the ward-month is a structural zero; otherwise counts follow Poisson or NB
Hurdle: a binary part (any case?) and a zero-truncated count part
Fit with pscl::zeroinfl(y ~ x | z, dist = "negbin"): the part after | models pi

title: Session 4 — Excess Zeros and Model Checking
text:
Fitting it

m_zinb <- zeroinfl(cases ~ fogging + slum + rain_lag1 + month_index + sin(2 * pi * month / 12) + cos(2 * pi * month / 12) + offset(log(population)) | 1, data = dg, dist = "negbin")
c(structural_zero_probability = round(plogis(coef(m_zinb, "zero")), 3)); AIC(m_nb, m_zinb)

structural_zero_probability.(Intercept) 
                                   0.06 


       df      AIC
m_nb    8 5898.446
m_zinb  9 5871.452

title: Session 4 — Excess Zeros and Model Checking
text:
Be cautious


AIC improves, but only modestly here (about 27 points)
First look for a covariate that explains the zeros (a reporting-quality indicator): the zero part can then use it (| reporting)
Do not add a mixture just because there are zeros: ask why
Interpretation: the count part gives rate ratios among at-risk ward-months

title: Session 4 — Excess Zeros and Model Checking
Session 4 — Excess Zeros and Model Checking
text: Observed against fitted, over time

title: Session 4 — Excess Zeros and Model Checking
text:
Leftover correlation

w1 <- dg$ward == levels(dg$ward)[1]
round(acf(residuals(m_nb, type = "pearson")[w1], plot = FALSE)$acf[1:4], 2)

[1]  1.00  0.13  0.04 -0.06



Autocorrelation of residuals within a ward: lag 1 is 0.13, so consecutive months are somewhat dependent
Consequence: standard errors slightly optimistic; fix with clustered robust SEs, random effects, or time-series terms (lagged cases)
Also check residuals by predictor and by ward

title: Session 4 — Excess Zeros and Model Checking
text:
Model-checking checklist


Dispersion and zeros: observed vs expected
Observed vs predicted over time
Autocorrelation of residuals
Influential wards: refit leaving one ward out
Sensitivity: Poisson, NB, zero-inflated: do the rate ratios agree?

text:
Self-check quiz (1/5)

A negative binomial model expects 19% zeros and 20% are observed. What should you conclude?

Only a small excess, so a zero-inflated model is not clearly needed
The model has failed completely and its output is of no use
The data cannot be analysed with a count model of any type
Every ward has the same chance of recording a zero in a month

title: Session 4 — Excess Zeros and Model Checking
text:
Self-check quiz (2/5)

What is a structural zero?

A zero from a process that cannot produce counts, such as non-reporting
A zero that arises by chance because the mean count is small
A zero caused by a coding error in the file that should be fixed
Any month of the series with fewer than five cases in the ward

title: Session 4 — Excess Zeros and Model Checking
text:
Self-check quiz (3/5)

In a zero-inflated model, the part after the vertical bar models what?

The probability of a structural zero (the zero-inflation part)
The mean of the count process for the ward-months at risk
The offset, which is the log of the population of the ward
The dispersion parameter theta of the negative binomial part

title: Session 4 — Excess Zeros and Model Checking
text:
Self-check quiz (4/5)

What is the best first step when a model shows more zeros than expected?

Find out why, and look for a covariate that explains them
Add a zero-inflation term straight away without more thought
Delete every row that contains a zero count from the data
Switch to linear regression on the log of the monthly counts

title: Session 4 — Excess Zeros and Model Checking
text:
Self-check quiz (5/5)

Residuals of a ward over successive months have lag-1 autocorrelation 0.13. What does that imply?

Months are dependent; standard errors are optimistic
The model is perfect and no further checks are needed at all
The ward must be removed from the data before the next fit
The offset has the wrong sign in the model that was fitted

title: Session 4 — Excess Zeros and Model Checking
text:
Score and take-home
Your score: 

Compare observed and expected zeros from the fitted model
Structural zeros need a reason (reporting); not every excess needs a mixture
zeroinfl(y ~ x | z, dist = negbin); compare AIC and rate ratios
Check fit over time, autocorrelation and influential wards

title: Ordinal and Multinomial Outcomes Cheat Sheet
Ordinal and Multinomial Outcomes Cheat Sheet
text:
1 · Which model?









Outcome
Example
Model
R




Ordered, 3+ categories
anaemia grade, BP stage
Ordinal logistic (proportional odds)
MASS::polr(y ~ x, Hess = TRUE)


… if the assumption fails for few predictors

Partial proportional odds
ordinal::clm(y ~ x, nominal = ~ z)


Nominal, 3+ categories
place of delivery
Multinomial logistic
nnet::multinom(y ~ x) (set the reference)


Binary
any anaemia
Logistic
glm(family = binomial)



Check first: order meaningful? Smallest category big enough (here 103 women)? Never code categories 1-4 for linear regression.

title: Ordinal and Multinomial Outcomes Cheat Sheet
text:
2 · Ordinal logistic







Item
Meaning




logit P(Y <= k) = zeta_k - x*beta
one threshold per cut-point (K - 1), one beta per predictor


exp(beta)
odds ratio for a higher category, the same at every cut-point


polr beta > 0
higher (worse) categories more likely


Our result: wealth
OR 0.76 per quintile: 24% lower odds of a worse category

title: Ordinal and Multinomial Outcomes Cheat Sheet
text:
3 · Checking proportional odds







Tool
What it shows




brant(model)
omnibus p and one p per predictor; here omnibus p = 0.000, tribal p = 0.000, wealth p = 0.57


Binary models at each cut
glm(I(y >= k) ~ x) for each k: ORs should be similar


LR test anova(clm_po, clm_partial)
does freeing a predictor improve the fit?


If it fails
partial PO for the offending predictor, cut-specific ORs, or multinomial

title: Ordinal and Multinomial Outcomes Cheat Sheet
text:
4 · Multinomial logistic







Item
Meaning




K - 1 equations vs the reference
each predictor has K - 1 coefficients


exp(coef)
relative risk ratio (odds vs the reference)


Our result: wealth
RRR 1.50 (PHC), 1.78 (public), 2.76 (private), each vs Home


No p-values printed
z = coef / SE: s <- summary(mn); s$coefficients / s$standard.errors


A whole variable
likelihood-ratio test: anova(model_without, model_with)


Reference
changes presentation, not the fit

title: Ordinal and Multinomial Outcomes Cheat Sheet
text:
5 · Showing results
predict(model, newdata, type = "probs") gives the probability of each category (adds to 1). Plot against a key predictor. Do not judge by accuracy (0.48 here vs 0.32 for guessing).

title: Ordinal and Multinomial Outcomes Cheat Sheet
text:
6 · Pitfalls


Categories coded 1-4 in linear regression; dichotomising needlessly
No assumption check; a single OR that hides a violation (tribal group here: OR about 1.1, but about 3 for severe anaemia)
Sparse categories; a multinomial model with too many parameters for the sample
RRR read as a risk ratio; accuracy as the measure of fit
Association read as cause

title: Ordinal and Multinomial Outcomes Cheat Sheet
text:
7 · One-paragraph report
Among 1,500 women, anaemia (none, mild, moderate, severe) was modelled with a proportional-odds model adjusted for education, BMI, antenatal visits, parity, age, tribal group and residence. Each higher wealth quintile was associated with 24% lower odds of a worse category (OR 0.76). The Brant test rejected proportional odds for tribal group only (p < 0.001), whose effect was concentrated on severe anaemia, so it is reported by cut-point. Place of delivery was modelled with a multinomial logit (reference: home): each wealth quintile multiplied the relative risk of private-hospital delivery 2.8-fold.

title: Session 2 — Ordinal Logistic Regression
text:
Where we are

Session 1: ordered vs nominal outcomes; cumulative proportions
Today: the proportional-odds model for an ordered outcome
By the end you can:

fit it with MASS::polr and read odds ratios
explain the thresholds
give predicted probabilities for each category

title: Session 2 — Ordinal Logistic Regression
text:
Cumulative logits

logit P(Y ≤ k) = ζk − (β1x1 + β2x2 + …) k = 1, 2, 3


One threshold ζk for each cut-point between categories (3 for 4 categories)
One set of coefficients β shared by all cut-points: the proportional-odds (parallel lines) assumption
exp(β) is the odds ratio for being in a higher category: the same whichever cut-point you look at
In polr, β > 0 means higher categories (worse anaemia) are more likely

title: Session 2 — Ordinal Logistic Regression
text:
One predictor

m1 <- MASS::polr(anaemia ~ wealth, data = mat, Hess = TRUE)
round(exp(cbind(OR = coef(m1), confint(m1))), 2)

         OR     
2.5 %  0.57 0.53
97.5 % 0.57 0.63

m1$zeta |> round(2)

      None|Mild   Mild|Moderate Moderate|Severe 
          -1.39            0.00            1.21 



OR = 0.57 per wealth quintile: each quintile higher multiplies the odds of being in a worse anaemia category by about 0.57 (a 43% reduction), at every cut-point (None vs worse, up to Moderate vs Severe).

title: Session 2 — Ordinal Logistic Regression
text:
Several predictors

m2 <- MASS::polr(anaemia ~ wealth + education + bmi + anc_visits + parity + age + tribal + residence, data = mat, Hess = TRUE)
round(exp(cbind(OR = coef(m2), confint(m2))), 2)     # tbl_regression(m2, exponentiate = TRUE) formats this for a paper

                     OR 2.5 % 97.5 %
wealth             0.76  0.68   0.85
educationPrimary   0.75  0.57   0.99
educationSecondary 0.62  0.45   0.86
educationHigher    0.46  0.31   0.66
bmi                0.93  0.90   0.96
anc_visits         0.90  0.84   0.95
parity             1.11  1.01   1.21
age                1.01  1.00   1.03
tribalYes          1.11  0.83   1.48
residenceRural     1.21  0.94   1.56

title: Session 2 — Ordinal Logistic Regression
text:
Reading the adjusted odds ratios

Wealth, higher education, BMI and antenatal visits are protective (OR below 1)
Parity goes slightly the other way
The OR for tribal group is only about 1.1: do not trust it yet. Session 3 shows the model is wrong for that variable
confint() gives profile-likelihood CIs; p-values come from the t value (|t| above about 2)

title: Session 2 — Ordinal Logistic Regression
text:
Thresholds

None|Mild: ζ1 Mild|Moderate: ζ2 Moderate|Severe: ζ3

They are the baseline log-odds of each cumulative probability (when all predictors are 0) and are not of substantive interest. K categories need K − 1 thresholds.

title: Session 2 — Ordinal Logistic Regression
section: What it means for a woman
text:
What it means for a woman

nd <- data.frame(wealth = c(1, 5), education = factor("Primary", levels = levels(mat$education)), bmi = 20.5, anc_visits = 3, parity = 2, age = 27,
                 tribal = factor("No", levels = c("No", "Yes")), residence = factor("Rural", levels = c("Urban", "Rural")))
rownames(nd) <- c("poorest", "richest")
round(predict(m2, newdata = nd, type = "probs"), 2)

        None Mild Moderate Severe
poorest 0.38 0.34     0.18   0.10
richest 0.65 0.24     0.08   0.03



Probability of each category for a given profile: the four numbers add to 1
The poorest woman has about a 10% chance of severe anaemia; the richest about 3%
Clearer for readers than odds ratios: report both

title: Session 2 — Ordinal Logistic Regression
text:
Compared with a binary model

c(ordinal = unname(exp(coef(m1))), binary_any_vs_none = unname(exp(coef(glm(I(anaemia != "None") ~ wealth, family = binomial, data = mat)))["wealth"])) |> round(2)

           ordinal binary_any_vs_none 
              0.57               0.57 


When proportional odds holds, the ordinal and the binary ORs agree, but the ordinal model uses the severity too, so it is more precise.

title: Session 2 — Ordinal Logistic Regression
text:
Reporting an ordinal model


State the outcome order and the model (cumulative-logit, proportional odds)
Odds ratios with CIs, and say they are for a higher category
A few predicted probabilities
The assumption check (next session)

A proportional-odds model gives OR = 0.57 per wealth quintile. Which is the best reading?

Each quintile higher lowers the anaemia grade by 0.57 categories on average
Women in the top quintile have 57% of the anaemia of the poorest women
Each quintile higher multiplies the odds of a worse category by 0.57

title: Session 2 — Ordinal Logistic Regression
text:
Self-check quiz (2/5)

Why does a model for a four-category outcome have three thresholds?

Three of the four categories are used up as references
There are three cut-points between four ordered categories
The model needs one separate threshold for each predictor
Four categories need four thresholds minus one for the intercept

title: Session 2 — Ordinal Logistic Regression

What is the proportional-odds assumption?

The categories of the outcome are equally spaced in terms of severity
The predictors are proportional to the outcome on the log-odds scale
Each predictor’s effect is the same at every cut-point of the outcome
The odds of each single category are equal in all of the groups

title: Session 2 — Ordinal Logistic Regression
text:
Self-check quiz (4/5)

Why are predicted probabilities useful alongside odds ratios?

They are always more accurate than the odds ratios from the same model
They remove the need to check the model assumptions of the analysis
They show whether each of the thresholds is significant or not
They give the chance of each category on a scale readers understand

text:

In polr, a positive coefficient for a predictor means what?

Higher values make the higher (worse) categories more likely
Higher values make the lower categories more likely to be seen
The predictor is significant at the 5% level in the sample
The predictor reduces all of the thresholds to exactly zero

title: Session 2 — Ordinal Logistic Regression
text:
Score and take-home
Your score: 

Proportional-odds: one OR per predictor, the same at every cut-point
exp(β) = odds of a higher category; K categories → K − 1 thresholds
Report ORs with CI and predicted probabilities
The single OR is only trustworthy if the assumption holds

title: Session 4 — Multinomial Logistic Regression
text:
Where we are

Sessions 2-3: ordered outcomes and their assumption
Today: nominal outcomes, with no ordering: place of delivery
By the end you can:

fit nnet::multinom and choose a reference category
read relative risk ratios and test them
get predicted probabilities

title: Session 4 — Multinomial Logistic Regression
section: A set of logistic models against a reference
text:
A set of logistic models against a reference

log [ P(Y = j) / P(Y = Home) ] = β0j + β1j x1 + … for j = PHC, Public, Private


K − 1 equations (3 for 4 places), each comparing a category with the reference
Every predictor has a different coefficient in each equation
exp(βj) is a relative risk ratio (an odds ratio versus the reference)
Fitted jointly by maximum likelihood: the probabilities add to 1

title: Session 4 — Multinomial Logistic Regression
text:
Fit it

mat$delivery <- relevel(mat$delivery, ref = "Home")
mn <- nnet::multinom(delivery ~ wealth + education + anc_visits + residence + tribal, data = mat, trace = FALSE)
round(exp(coef(mn)[, "wealth"]), 2)

             PHC  Public hospital Private hospital 
            1.50             1.78             2.76 



Each wealth quintile multiplies the odds of delivering in a private hospital rather than at home by 2.76, in a public hospital by 1.78, in a PHC by 1.5. Wealth pulls women away from home, and most strongly towards private care.

title: Session 4 — Multinomial Logistic Regression
text:
The output has no p-values

s <- summary(mn); z <- s$coefficients / s$standard.errors
round(2 * pnorm(-abs(z)), 4)[, c("wealth", "anc_visits", "residenceRural")]

                 wealth anc_visits residenceRural
PHC                   0          0         0.3621
Public hospital       0          0         0.0710
Private hospital      0          0         0.0007


Compute z = coefficient / SE and the two-sided p-value. For a variable with several coefficients (education has 3 per equation), use a likelihood-ratio test of the whole variable:

mn0 <- nnet::multinom(delivery ~ wealth + anc_visits + residence + tribal, data = mat, trace = FALSE)
anova(mn0, mn)

title: Session 4 — Multinomial Logistic Regression
text:
Predicted probabilities

nd <- data.frame(wealth = c(1, 5), education = factor("Secondary", levels = levels(mat$education)), anc_visits = 4, residence = factor("Urban", levels = c("Urban", "Rural")), tribal = factor("No", levels = c("No", "Yes")))
rownames(nd) <- c("poorest", "richest"); round(predict(mn, newdata = nd, type = "probs"), 2)

        Home  PHC Public hospital Private hospital
poorest 0.22 0.37            0.37             0.04
richest 0.03 0.22            0.45             0.31



The poorest woman delivers mostly in public hospitals or PHCs (37% each) and only 4% in private care
The richest: 31% private, 3% at home
The probabilities tell the story more clearly than 9 odds ratios

title: Session 4 — Multinomial Logistic Regression
text:
The choice of reference

It changes which comparisons are shown, not the model: the fitted probabilities and log-likelihood are identical
Choose a large, meaningful group (here Home) so the comparisons make sense
Any other comparison (Private vs Public) = the difference of two coefficients; refit with another reference to get its CI

title: Session 4 — Multinomial Logistic Regression
text:
Pitfalls


Reading RRRs as risk ratios when the outcome is common (they are odds-type ratios)
Sparse categories (a few women in one place) make estimates unstable
Many parameters: 3 equations x every predictor needs a large sample
Ignoring the independence of irrelevant alternatives (adding or removing a category can change the others: be cautious with similar categories)
